name: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems
org_or_authors: Jinyuan Fang, Yanwen Peng, Xi Zhang, Yingxu Wang, Xinhao Yi, Guibin Zhang, Yi Xu, Bin Wu, Siwei Liu, Zihao Li, Zhaochun Ren, Nikos Aletras, Xi Wang, Han Zhou, Zaiqiao Meng (University of Glasgow-led; EvoAgentX team; co-authors from Sheffield, Leiden, Cambridge, etc.)
last_activity: Companion awesome-list last push 2026-05-16 (still merging PRs adding 2026 papers, e.g. CORAL, ReasoningBank); EvoAgentX framework repo last push 2026-08-27
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint (no peer-reviewed venue as of 2026-09). Citation count could not be verified (Semantic Scholar rate-limited; OpenAlex shows only 5, a known undercount for arXiv). Proxy impact: companion repo EvoAgentX/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Agents 2,477 stars / 190 forks; sibling framework EvoAgentX 3,317 stars (EMNLP'25 Demo paper).
mechanism: This is a survey, so the 'mechanism' is an abstraction, not a runnable loop. The paper's Figure 1 (verified from the repo asset) defines a 4-node cycle: (1) System Inputs I — task-level {T, D_train, D_test} or instance-level {x, y, C (context)}; (2) Agent System A — single-agent (prompt, tools, memory) or multi-agent (agents, communication, topology); (3) Environment — scenarios (coding, legal, research, medicine) that return Proxy Metrics: accuracy/F1/success rate or LLM-based evaluators; (4) Optimiser P = Search Space S (prompt template, tool selection, LLM parameters, architecture) x Optimisation Algorithm H (rule-based heuristics, gradient descent/text-gradients, Bayesian/MCTS/RL, learned policy). Edges: I -Setup-> A -Execution-> Env -Feedback-> P -Mutation-> A, plus a dashed P -Refine-> I edge (optimiser can alter the inputs/data). The taxonomy then classifies methods by which S they mutate: LLM behaviour (SFT/RL vs test-time feedback/search), prompts (edit/evolutionary/generative/text-gradient), memory, tools (training, inference-time selection, tool creation), and multi-agent (prompt-level, topology/workflow search e.g. AFlow/ADAS/GPTSwarm, unified, backbone fine-tuning). It frames a historical progression MOP -> MOA -> MAO -> MASE (Multi-Agent Self-Evolving) and proposes 'Three Laws': Endure (safety/stability during modification), Excel (preserve or improve performance), Evolve (autonomously optimise subject to the first two). The only concrete instantiation is the authors' EvoAgentX, which wraps TextGrad, MIPRO, AFlow and EvoPrompt as optimisers over a workflow graph: Original -> best optimiser: HotPotQA F1 63.6->71.0 (TextGrad), MBPP 69->79 (AFlow), MATH 66->76 (TextGrad), using 50 validation / 100 test samples.
eval_loop: In the abstraction, the Environment emits proxy metrics (accuracy, F1, success rate) computed on D_train/D_test at task level, or on a single (x, y) at instance level; where no ground truth exists, LLM-as-a-Judge / Agent-as-a-Judge provide the score. The survey's Evaluation section is a catalogue of static benchmarks (ToolBench, WebArena, SWE-bench, GAIA, OSWorld, AgentBench, MLGym) plus judge paradigms plus safety benchmarks (AgentHarm, RedCode, MACHIAVELLI, R-Judge, AGrail). Drift / reward-hacking prevention is addressed only normatively via the 'Endure' and 'Excel' laws and a call for 'evolution-aware audits' and continuous monitoring; the paper itself flags 'reward modeling scarcity destabilizes behavior' as an open problem. No held-out generalisation protocol, regression test, or rollback mechanism is specified. In EvoAgentX the signal is a fixed benchmark split (50 val / 100 test) with best-on-validation selection.
limitations: Survey-only: no experiments, no formal guarantees; the 4-node framework is descriptive and the 'Refine' (optimiser->inputs) and 'Mutation' edges are never formalised as operators. The Three Laws are Asimov-style aspirations with no enforcement mechanism (no versioning, rollback, canary evaluation, sandboxing, or human approval gates discussed). Evaluation section lists benchmarks for agents, not metrics for evolution itself (learning curves across rounds, forgetting, transfer). Taxonomy is prompt/topology-heavy and 2025-arXiv-heavy; agent-source-code self-modification (Darwin Godel Machine), Voyager-style skill libraries, and quality-diversity archives are thin or absent. 'Lifelong' in the title is not matched by coverage of continual deployment loops; the only instantiation (EvoAgentX) is offline, one-shot optimisation on tiny splits. Competes with and largely overlaps the earlier Gao et al. survey (arXiv 2507.21046, July 2025) which it cites but does not compare against. Full HTML/PDF could not be fetched directly (arXiv connection resets); details verified via abstract page, repo figure/README, and third-party summaries.
key_insight: Every self-evolving agent system reduces to one cycle — Inputs -> Agent System -> Environment (proxy metric) -> Optimiser -> mutate Agent System — where 'what evolves' is just the chosen Search Space S (prompt / tools / memory / weights / topology) and 'how' is the algorithm H (heuristic / text-gradient / MCTS / RL); a harness should therefore make S and H pluggable and keep the evaluator separate from both.
open_gaps: No formalisation of the Optimiser->Inputs 'Refine' edge: task/curriculum self-generation is drawn in the figure but never taxonomised or given an operator; a framework could make curriculum evolution a first-class, evaluated component

Evaluation of evolution itself is absent: no metrics for per-round improvement, regression rate, catastrophic forgetting, or held-out cross-task transfer of evolved prompts/workflows (fitness = single benchmark split)
'Endure' and 'Excel' laws have no enforcement mechanism: no versioned artifact store, rollback, canary/shadow evaluation, sandboxing of self-modifications, or human approval gate is described
Evaluator is treated as a fixed environment output; no coverage of evaluator co-evolution, judge robustness, or defenses against the agent gaming an LLM-as-judge signal
Single-loop abstraction ignores multiple loops at different timescales (instance-level test-time refinement vs task-level offline optimisation vs weight updates) and how they interact or conflict

Agent-source-code / harness self-modification (DGM-style), skill-library accumulation (Voyager-style), and quality-diversity archives/populations are missing or thin; search is framed as best-so-far only
No treatment of optimisation budget: token/compute cost per evolution round, stopping criteria, or cost-aware acceptance
Companion EvoAgentX instantiation is offline, one-shot (50 val / 100 test) with no continual/lifelong deployment loop despite 'lifelong' framing
No multi-tenant / production concerns: how evolved artifacts are promoted, A/B tested, or shared across users and tasks
safety_measures: Discussed normatively only: Three Laws (Endure = maintain safety/stability during modification; Excel = preserve performance; Evolve = autonomous optimisation subordinate to the first two); calls for continuous monitoring across the evolutionary lifecycle, 'evolution-aware audits and adaptive regulatory mechanisms', and notes that dynamic evolution undermines static legal/safety frameworks. Cites safety benchmarks (AgentHarm, RedCode, MobileSafetyBench, MACHIAVELLI, R-Judge, SafeLawBench) and lifelong guardrails/attacks (AGrail, AutoDAN-Turbo). No concrete technical mechanism (rollback, sandbox, constraint enforcement) is specified.
key_results: No experimental results (survey). Headline artifacts: unified 4-component feedback-loop framework (Inputs/Agent System/Environment/Optimiser with Search Space + Algorithm); Three Laws (Endure/Excel/Evolve); MOP->MOA->MAO->MASE progression; taxonomy across single-agent (LLM behaviour, prompt, memory, tool), multi-agent (prompt, topology, unified, backbone), domain-specific (biomedicine, programming, finance/law), evaluation (benchmarks, LLM/Agent-as-judge), safety. Companion EvoAgentX numbers (its own README): Original vs best optimiser HotPotQA F1 63.58->71.02 (TextGrad), MBPP pass@1 69->79 (AFlow), MATH 66->76 (TextGrad); also prompt-optimised Open Deep Research and OWL on GAIA validation.

name: A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence
org_or_authors: Huan-ang Gao, Jiayi Geng, Wenyue Hua, Mengkang Hu, Xinzhe Juan, Hongzhang Liu, Shilong Liu, Jiahao Qiu, ... Qingyun Wu, Heng Ji, Mengdi Wang (26 authors in v1, ~35 in v4; Princeton, Tsinghua, CMU, UIUC, Penn State, U. Sydney, and ~10 other institutions; corresponding: Mengdi Wang / Heng Ji)
date: v1 2025-07-28 (title 'On Path to Artificial Super Intelligence'); v4 2026-01-16 (retitled 'What, When, How, and Where to Evolve ...')
last_activity: Paper: v4 on 2026-01-16. Companion repo: last push 2025-10-15; community PRs/issues still being filed through 2026-06-14 but none merged since Oct 2025.
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint (cs.AI), no peer-reviewed venue found. OpenAlex reports 3 citations (clearly an undercount for a preprint; Semantic Scholar was rate-limited so its count could not be verified). Companion repo CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents: 1,313 stars, 106 forks. Widely referenced as the canonical taxonomy for the term 'self-evolving agent' (scout note), though a competing 'Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents' (arXiv 2508.07407) appeared two weeks later.
mechanism:
This is a survey, not a system: it proposes no loop of its own and runs no experiments. Its contribution is a formal frame plus a four-axis taxonomy for other people's loops.

Formalization: agent-environment interaction is a POMDP; an agent is a tuple of (architecture, model(s), context [memory + prompts], toolset). 'Self-evolution' is an update operator that rewrites one or more tuple components from observed trajectories and feedback so as to maximize cumulative utility over a task stream.

Taxonomy axes:
- WHAT to evolve: (1) model weights via self-generated supervision / env feedback (STaR, SELF, Self-Challenging, RAGEN); (2) context: memory evolution (Mem0, MemoryOS, Agent Workflow Memory) and prompt optimization (APE, OPRO, ProTeGi, PromptAgent, TextGrad, DSPy); (3) tools: creation/mastery/selection (Voyager, Alita, ATLASS, ToolGen); (4) architecture: single-agent workflow search (AgentSquare, ADAS, AFlow, Godel Agent, AlphaEvolve) and multi-agent topology/orchestration (EvoFlow, MaAS, ScoreFlow, FlowReasoner, ReMA).
- WHEN: intra-test-time (adaptation during a task via ICL/reflection, TTT, TTRL, SEAL) vs inter-test-time (retrospective learning between tasks: STaR, SiriuS, WebRL curriculum, DigiRL).
- HOW: reward-based (scalar env reward, textual critique, self-confidence/consistency, rule-based rewards, self-play), imitation/demonstration (self-generated, cross-agent, hybrid), population-based/evolutionary (Darwin Godel Machine, GA over LLM populations, SPIN/SPC self-play, evolving orchestration).
- WHERE: general (web/GUI/mobile assistants) vs specialized (coding, healthcare, education, finance).

Evaluation frame: five goals (adaptivity, retention, generalization, efficiency, safety) and three paradigms (static, short-horizon adaptive, long-horizon lifelong assessment).
eval_loop: None of its own. The survey catalogs signals used by others (env rewards, unit tests/SWE-bench, textual critiques, self-consistency/confidence, self-play win rates, LLM/agent-as-judge e.g. Mind2Web 2) and benchmarks (AgentBench, GAIA, SWE-bench, OSWorld, WebArena, MLE-bench, MCP-Universe, LifelongAgentBench, Agent-SafetyBench). Its normative contribution is to argue that adaptivity should be measured alongside retention (forgetting), generalization under shift, cost/efficiency, and safety, and that longitudinal, persistent-state, cost-aware evaluation is needed because 'most benchmarks use episodic evaluation that resets agent states', so cumulative learning and catastrophic forgetting are invisible. On drift/reward hacking it only names the risks ('misevolution', deployment-time reward hacking, unsafe self-created tools) and prescribes guardrails (sandboxing, automated verification of self-generated tools, immutable audit trails, tested rollback, monitoring, red-teaming, human approval gates); no metric, protocol, or formula is specified.
key_results: No empirical results. Deliverables: (a) a POMDP/agent-tuple formalization of self-evolution; (b) the What/When/How/Where taxonomy; (c) a five-goal, three-paradigm evaluation framework; (d) domain review (coding, GUI, healthcare, education, finance); (e) future-direction list (personalization/cold-start, generalization vs specialization, safe and controllable evolution, multi-agent ecosystems). Companion repo catalogs ~183 entries (~157 unique arXiv papers) organized by the taxonomy. Retitled and expanded in v4 (Jan 2026) to add the 'Where' axis and grew to ~35 authors.
limitations: Stated by authors: evaluation is 'the most underserved area'; retention/forgetting rarely measured; safety mechanisms for self-modifying agents underdeveloped; co-evolutionary multi-agent dynamics and theory of safe adaptation not addressed in depth. Observed: no unified benchmark or reproduction; the formalization is a thin POMDP restatement with no operational definition distinguishing 'self-evolution' from ordinary test-time refinement (Reflexion/Self-Refine are filed as intra-test-time evolution even though nothing persists); the 'path to ASI' framing is rhetorical; the companion repo is a link list with no code and has been effectively unmaintained since Oct 2025 (5 community PRs open since Jan-Jun 2026). 'Self-evolving' here is a taxonomy label, not a demonstrated capability.
key_insight: Treat self-evolution as an explicit update operator over a typed agent tuple (model, context, tools, architecture), classify every method by which component it rewrites, whether it fires inside a task or between tasks, and what signal drives it (reward / demonstration / population), and then evaluate not just adaptivity but retention, generalization, cost and safety over a persistent, non-resetting task stream.
safety_measures: Discussion only, no implementation: identifies misevolution (goal/alignment drift), deployment-time reward hacking of self-defined rewards, vulnerable/malicious self-generated tools, and memory privacy leakage; recommends sandboxing, automated security verification of self-created tools, immutable audit trails for every evolutionary change, tested rollback, continuous monitoring, automated red-teaming, and human approval gates for high-stakes changes. Cites TrustAgent, AgentDAM, Agent-SafetyBench, ST-WebAgentBench.
open_gaps: No executable reference implementation of the taxonomy: a framework could expose the agent tuple (model/context/tools/architecture) as typed, versioned mutable slots with a uniform evolve() interface
No benchmark or protocol for the 'retention' goal the survey calls most underserved: a persistent, non-resetting task stream that measures cumulative gain and forgetting across sessions
No cost-aware evaluation: the survey asks for efficiency metrics but gives none; a framework could log tokens/wall-clock per evolution step and report improvement-per-dollar
Guardrails (audit trail, rollback, tool verification, human approval gates) are prescribed but never operationalized; none of the cataloged systems ship an immutable change log with rollback
No treatment of when NOT to evolve: no trigger/gating policy that decides whether a task warrants a persistent update versus one-off in-context adaptation
Cross-component coupling is unexamined: nothing about co-evolving memory + tools + prompts jointly, or arbitration when updates to different slots conflict
No held-out generalization discipline: cataloged methods mostly optimize on the evaluation distribution; a framework could enforce train/holdout task splits for every accepted mutation
Reward-evaluator evolution (self-rewarding, self-play critics) is listed but the survey gives no defense against evaluator drift or Goodharting when the judge is itself mutable
Nearly all covered methods require either GPU fine-tuning or offline search; no lightweight, weight-free loop targeted at application developers running frontier APIs
Companion repo is a stale link list (no merges since Oct 2025); no living, machine-readable registry of self-evolving methods with reproducible results

name: ReasoningBank (+ MaTTS: memory-aware test-time scaling)
mechanism: Closed loop per task in a stream, with frozen weights and a fixed agent scaffold. (1) Retrieve: embed the new task query (gemini-embedding-001, 3072-d; Qwen3-Embedding-8B optional), cosine-score against cached embeddings of PAST TASK QUERIES (not memory items), take the top-1 prior task (code: select_memory(n=1)) and paste its memory items (<=3) into the system prompt with an instruction to "explicitly discuss if you want to use each memory item". (2) Act: BrowserGym/WebArena agent or mini-swe-agent runs the task. (3) Self-judge: an LLM labels the trajectory success/fail with no ground truth -- WebArena uses a prompt over last-5 page captions + think/action history; SWE-Bench uses a one-line "Did the agent succeed? answer success/fail" prompt at temp 0. (4) Extract: the backbone LLM (temp 1.0) is given the trajectory + judge rationale and one of two system prompts (SUCCESSFUL_SI / FAILED_SI) to emit <=3 items of {Title, Description (when/when-not to use), Content (1-3 sentences)}; failures yield "recovery procedures / pitfalls". (5) Consolidate: items are appended to a JSONL file keyed by task_id; no dedup, pruning, merging, scoring, or decay. MaTTS: parallel = run k trajectories per task (separate ports), pick answer by LLM best-of-N (paper), then induce memory from ALL k trajectories with a "self-contrast" prompt (PARALLEL_SI, <=5 items) that compares successes vs failures; sequential = re-prompt the agent to re-examine its own trajectory, using the intermediate reflections as memory signal. The claim is bidirectional: better memory makes scaling productive, and more diverse rollouts give richer contrastive signal for memory.
eval_loop: Improvement signal is purely the LLM self-judge (success/fail label, no ground truth, no test execution even on SWE-Bench) feeding a one-shot memory-extraction prompt. There is NO fitness gate on the memory itself: every extracted item is appended regardless of whether it later helps, there is no held-out check, no A/B of memory vs no-memory, no rollback, no dedup/contradiction resolution, and no exclusion of the current task from retrieval (issues #17/#36: reruns can retrieve memory from the same task instance). Reported metric = task success rate + avg steps on WebArena/Mind2Web/SWE-Bench-Verified, graded by a vendored, modified WebArena harness (lenient 'MemEvol' llm_fuzzy_match prompt with Gemini-2.5-pro instead of GPT-4-turbo, patched shopping annotations), so absolute numbers are not leaderboard-comparable. Paper says judge noise is tolerated empirically; drift/reward-hacking is not addressed beyond that.
limitations: Stated by authors: retrieval and consolidation are 'intentionally minimal'; judge dependence introduces noise; future work on compositional memory and learned controllers. Observed: (a) reproducibility is contested -- three independent reports (issues #2, #6, #11) find no gain or degradation vs no-memory on WebArena-Shopping with Gemini-2.5-Flash (e.g. 42.2->42.8 with GT reward; 50.05 no-memory vs 45.99 ReasoningBank via AI Studio; ~36-37% vs paper's 49.7%); another user found ReasoningBank ~= AWM on Qwen3.5. Authors acknowledged codebase errors, pushed a cleanup in Apr 2026, and results were obtained with a modified WebArena grader not originally in the repo. (b) Released code is incomplete vs paper: no sequential-MaTTS pipeline, no LLM best-of-N selector, parallel induction prompt omits success/fail labels, induce_scaling.py still has inverted 'reward==0 -> success' and reads the same results dir for every sample. (c) Memory bank is a flat append-only JSONL per website; retrieval is top-1 prior task by query similarity; bank grows linearly with no forgetting. (d) Benchmarks are sequential single-pass over a test stream, so 'learning' and 'evaluation' are on the same tasks (online setting), and cross-site transfer is not tested (memory files are per-website). (e) Only Gemini/Claude via Vertex supported cleanly. Google disclaimer: 'demonstration purposes only... not intended for production'.
key_insight: Store distilled, reusable reasoning strategies (title/description/content) rather than raw trajectories or success-only workflows, and mine FAILED trajectories for explicit pitfalls/recovery rules; then treat extra test-time rollouts as a source of contrastive signal for memory synthesis (memory <-> TTS synergy) rather than only as answer-selection.
open_gaps: No fitness/acceptance test for a memory item: items are appended unconditionally; a framework should score items by downstream lift (e.g. counterfactual replay or held-out tasks) and evict/rollback harmful ones
No consolidation: no dedup, merging, contradiction resolution, versioning, or decay -- bank grows linearly; template_id is stored 'for deduplication' but never used
Retrieval is top-1 prior TASK by query-embedding similarity, not retrieval over memory items themselves; no reranking, no usage/success statistics, no negative-result tracking
Self-judge is a single unverified LLM call (SWE-Bench: one-line 'success/fail' prompt) -- no test execution, no calibration, no confidence gating; mislabeled trajectories poison memory silently

Current-task/self-retrieval contamination not guarded (issue #17/#36 open); evaluation protocol conflates online learning on the test stream with generalization -- no train/test split, no cross-website or cross-domain transfer of one bank
Memory is per-website/per-model text; no cross-task, cross-environment, or cross-agent sharing, and no mechanism to evolve tools/skills/code, only prompt-injected text

Sequential MaTTS and LLM best-of-N selector described in the paper are not in the released code; parallel-induction script has an inverted success label -- an implementable, tested reference loop is missing

Reported gains rely on a modified, lenient WebArena grader (Gemini-2.5-pro fuzzy match) and are not reproduced by three independent groups -- a new framework needs a standardized, GT-verified eval harness with ablations against no-memory at equal token budget

Absolute numbers depend on Vertex AI-hosted Gemini; no open-weight reproduction; token/cost overhead of memory extraction (extra LLM calls per task, k-fold under MaTTS) is only reported as +4.3% inference tokens
No safety layer: no filtering of memory content, no protection against adversarial/injected memory, no human review, no rollback

name: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
last_activity: 2026-09-11 (gepa-ai/gepa repo push; paper v2 camera-ready 2026-02-14; artifact repo last push 2026-02-08)
org_or_authors: Lakshya A Agrawal, Shangyin Tan, Dilara Soylu, Noah Ziems, Rishi Khare, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Arnav Singhvi, Herumb Shandilya, Michael J Ryan, Meng Jiang, Christopher Potts, Koushik Sen, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Ion Stoica, Dan Klein, Matei Zaharia, Omar Khattab — UC Berkeley, Stanford, BespokeLabs.ai, Notre Dame, Databricks, MIT
venue_or_citations: ICLR 2026 Oral (OpenReview RQm2KQTM5r); earlier FoRLM 2025 workshop version. arXiv v1 25 Jul 2025, v2 (camera-ready) 14 Feb 2026. Exact citation count not retrievable during this read (Semantic Scholar API rate-limited; OpenAlex record is stale), but it is the standard baseline in 2026 prompt-optimizer papers. Code: gepa-ai/gepa (6,518 stars, 543 forks, ~47 contributors, MIT, v0.1.4 Jul 2026) + reproduction artifact gepa-ai/gepa-artifact (35 stars).
mechanism: Paper scope: only the natural-language instruction of each LLM module in a compound program evolves (the library's later optimize_anything / gskill extend the same loop to code, agent architectures and skills). Offline outer loop over a fixed metric-call budget (matched to MIPROv2-Heavy: e.g. 6,871 calls on HotpotQA; IFBench used 678 rollouts). State = a growing tree of candidate programs, each with per-instance scores on a validation set. Per iteration (verified in artifact code): (1) SELECT parent from the per-instance Pareto front: for every val instance collect the best-scoring candidates, drop dominated ones, sample a candidate with probability proportional to the number of instances it wins (ablation 'SelectBestCandidate' = greedy argmax). (2) Pick one module round-robin. (3) Run parent on a minibatch of 3 training examples, capturing that module's inputs, outputs, reasoning and a task-specific textual feedback function mu_f (missing retrieved docs, failed IFBench constraint, judge rationale). (4) REFLECT: a reflection LM (GPT-4.1 / GPT-5 in practice) receives current instruction + examples/outputs/feedback and writes a new instruction; the static prompt tells it to infer the task, extract 'niche domain-specific facts' and generalizable strategies. (5) Evaluate the child on the same minibatch; accept only if the summed score strictly improves; then evaluate on the full valset, add to the pool, update the Pareto front. (6) MERGE (optional, max 5 invocations): after an accepted mutation, take two Pareto candidates sharing an ancestor that improved different modules, splice modules, test on instances where the parents disagree, keep if >= both parents, then full-val evaluate. Output = candidate with best aggregate val score, reported on held-out test. The reflection LM and its prompt never change.
eval_loop: Signal = user-supplied task metric mu (exact match / F1 / constraint pass / LLM-judge for PUPA) plus a textual feedback function mu_f fed to the reflector ('actionable side information'). Three gates against drift: (a) child must strictly beat parent on the same 3-example minibatch (cheap, noisy), (b) accepted children get a full validation-set evaluation and only the per-instance val scores drive future selection, (c) per-instance Pareto front keeps diverse lineages alive instead of collapsing to one greedy trajectory (ablation on Qwen3-8B: 61.28 vs 54.89 aggregate). Reporting is on a held-out test split. No statistical test on acceptance, no multi-seed runs, no explicit reward-hacking check: the reflection prompt actively encourages baking 'niche factual information' from training feedback into the prompt, so overfitting to the train/val distribution is checked only by the held-out test at the end. Reflection-LM token cost is not counted in the rollout budget.
key_results: Artifact notebook (matches v1 Table 1), test-set scores. Qwen3-8B (HotpotQA/IFBench/PUPA/HoVer/aggregate): Baseline 42.33/36.90/80.82/35.33/48.84; MIPROv2 55.33/36.22/81.55/47.33/55.11; GRPO (24,000 rollouts, LoRA) 43.33/35.88/86.66/38.67/51.14; GEPA 62.33/38.61/91.85/52.33/61.28; GEPA+Merge 64.33/28.23/86.26/51.67/57.62. GPT-4.1-mini (AIME/HotpotQA/IFBench/LiveBenchMath/PUPA/HoVer/agg): Baseline 49.33/38.00/47.79/58.20/78.57/46.33/53.78; MIPROv2 51.33/58.00/49.15/61.84/83.37/48.33/60.14; GEPA 59.33/69.00/52.72/59.43/94.47/51.67/65.46; GEPA+Merge -/65.67/55.95/64.13/96.46/56.67/67.78. GRPO was only run on Qwen3-8B. v1 abstract: +10% avg over GRPO, up to +20% (HotpotQA 62.33 vs 43.33), up to 35x fewer rollouts (IFBench 678 vs 24,000; up to 78x counting training rollouts only), >10% over MIPROv2, prompts up to 9.2x shorter (artifact: ~1.3-1.5k vs ~6.3-6.5k tokens). v2 (ICLR camera-ready) abstract revises the GRPO margin to '6% on average and up to 20%'. Pareto vs greedy-selection ablation: +6.4 aggregate on Qwen3-8B (61.28 vs 54.89); on GPT-4.1-mini the greedy ablation is marginally higher (65.13 vs 64.44 in the artifact notebook). Also used as inference-time search for AMD NPU kernel / CUDA kernel optimization (qualitative wins, no headline number recoverable). Library follow-ups (not in paper): +10pp AIME with GPT-4.1-mini (46.6 to 56.6), 32% to 89% ARC-AGI agent-architecture search, 55% to 82% coding-agent resolve rate via learned skills.
limitations: (1) The headline average margin over GRPO was revised from 10% (v1) to 6% (v2 camera-ready) while the public artifact still holds v1 numbers; GRPO baseline is a single LoRA run on one 8B model with 8,192 context and 24k rollouts, no hyperparameter sweep, and GRPO was not run on GPT-4.1-mini. (2) Single-seed results, no confidence intervals. (3) System-aware merge hurts on Qwen3-8B (IFBench 38.61 to 28.23; aggregate 61.28 to 57.62), and Pareto selection only clearly beats greedy on Qwen3-8B, not GPT-4.1-mini. (4) Requires a hand-written per-module textual feedback function mu_f; the paper's gains lean on rich feedback, robustness to scalar-only signals is untested. (5) Only instructions evolve, not demos, code, topology or weights (in the paper). (6) Acceptance on a 3-example minibatch is noisy; candidate pool grows unboundedly with full-valset evals per accepted child. (7) Budget counts task-LM metric calls only; reflection-LM (GPT-4.1/GPT-5) cost and the need for a strong reflector are hidden. (8) Reflection prompt encourages memorizing domain facts from training feedback, i.e. distribution-specific prompts; no cross-task or cross-model transfer shown. (9) Round-robin module choice, no credit assignment across modules.
safety_measures: Strict-improvement acceptance on the same minibatch; full validation evaluation of every accepted candidate with per-instance score tracking; Pareto-front selection to avoid collapse; held-out test set for reporting; candidates are immutable tree nodes so the final pick is the best-by-validation (implicit rollback). No content/safety filter on generated prompts, no check for validation leakage into prompts, no adversarial or reward-hacking audit; reflection LM is trusted.
key_insight: Execution traces plus textual evaluator feedback are a far denser learning signal than a scalar reward: an LLM reflecting on a handful of failed trajectories can write rules that generalize, and keeping a per-instance Pareto frontier of candidates (rather than the single best) preserves complementary lessons so the search does not collapse — yielding RL-beating accuracy with ~35x fewer rollouts and no gradient updates.
open_gaps: Only module instructions evolve in the paper; no joint evolution of code, tool set, workflow topology or weights (library's optimize_anything extends this but without the paper's controlled evaluation).
No cross-task or cross-model transfer: learned lessons live inside a task/model-specific prompt and every new task or LM starts from the seed prompt; no reusable memory/skill store across runs.
Fitness is a fixed offline train/val split; no continual or online mode that ingests production traces, detects drift, or re-optimizes incrementally.

Acceptance uses a 3-example minibatch with a strict-improvement rule and no statistical test; noisy accepts are filtered only by a costly full-valset eval, and the candidate pool grows without pruning.
Requires a hand-authored per-module textual feedback function (mu_f); no automatic synthesis of actionable feedback from raw traces or from scalar-only metrics.
Reflection LM and reflection prompt are static and never improved (no meta-level self-improvement, no learning of what kinds of reflections lead to accepted mutations).

No verification/safety layer on proposed prompts: nothing checks for validation-set leakage, memorized answers, or unsafe instructions before acceptance; reflection prompt explicitly encourages baking in domain facts.
Reflection-LM token cost is excluded from the rollout budget; a cost-aware budget (task + reflection tokens) and cheaper reflectors are unaddressed.
Module selection is round-robin; no credit assignment deciding which module caused a failure, and merge is a fixed-count heuristic that regressed on Qwen3-8B.
GRPO comparison is one LoRA run on one 8B model; no study of combining prompt evolution with weight updates (the authors' May 2026 'Fast-Slow' blog only starts this).

name: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
org_or_authors: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Anima Anandkumar — NVIDIA, Caltech, UT Austin, Stanford, UW Madison/ASU
last_activity: Repo last substantive commit 2023-07-27 (dependency pins); last push 2024-04-03; effectively unmaintained
venue_or_citations: arXiv 2305.16291; published in TMLR (2024); NeurIPS 2023 workshop presentation; several thousand citations (Google Scholar, est. 3000+ by 2026) — the canonical reference for LLM 'skill library' agents
mechanism: Single-agent outer loop (voyager.py learn(), 160 iterations, 3 seeds). Each iteration: (1) CurriculumAgent (GPT-4, temp 0) proposes ONE next task from current state (biome, nearby/recently-seen blocks, entities, health/hunger, inventory, chests), the list of completed tasks and "failed tasks that are too hard", plus 5 self-asked questions answered by GPT-3.5 (cached in a Chroma vectordb). Observation fields are unlocked on a warm-up schedule; first task is hardcoded "Mine 1 wood log"; inventory-full triggers hardcoded chest tasks. (2) SkillManager retrieves top-5 skills by cosine similarity between the task context (+ summarized chat log on later rounds) and OpenAI embeddings of GPT-3.5-written descriptions of each stored program. (3) ActionAgent (GPT-4) writes one async Mineflayer JS function, given retrieved skill code, hand-written control primitives (mineBlock, craftItem, smeltItem, placeItem, killMob, exploreUntil), last-round code, execution error, chat log, state, and the critic's critique; code is babel-parsed, the last async function becomes the candidate skill. (4) The env executes it with ALL stored skills + primitives loaded as helper programs. (5) CriticAgent (GPT-4) judges success from the post-execution state only (inventory/equipment/health/hunger/nearby blocks/chests) and returns JSON {success, critique}; any execution error short-circuits to failure. Up to 4 rounds per task. (6) On success, program code + generated description are appended to skills.json/vectordb (name collision => overwrite, old file kept as V2); on failure after 4 rounds the task joins the failed list, which the curriculum reads. Skills are never modified, pruned, or re-validated afterward.
eval_loop: Per-task binary success from a GPT-4 critic (LLM judge) reading ground-truth Minecraft state after execution, plus hard signals from the environment: JS execution errors and bot.chat logs from Mineflayer. No scalar reward. A skill enters the library only after the critic says success; failed tasks are retried at most 4 rounds with critique/errors fed back, then recorded as "too hard" for the curriculum. Anti-drift/anti-hacking is weak and mostly structural: inventory is real environment state (can't be faked by text), code must parse and run, and the curriculum prompt explicitly forbids proposing tasks the critic can't verify from inventory (placing/building/planting/trading). Prompt-level 'do not cheat' rules (maxDistance 32, no infinite loops) are the only guardrails against gaming. No held-out evaluation of stored skills, no regression testing when a same-named skill is overwritten, no re-validation when a skill is reused in a new world. Paper-level evaluation: unique items obtained, tech-tree milestone iteration counts, map traversal, and zero-shot transfer of the library to unseen tasks in a fresh world. Ablations (paper): removing self-verification cuts unique items ~73%; random curriculum ~93% fewer; no skill library plateaus late; GPT-3.5 for code gives 5.7x fewer items; environment feedback and execution errors matter less than self-verification.
key_results: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations vs <20 for ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT (3.3x); tech-tree milestones unlocked 15.3x faster (wooden), 8.5x (stone), 6.4x (iron), and only Voyager reached diamond tools; 2.3x longer map traversal; zero-shot generalization: with the learned library it solved all 4 unseen tasks (diamond pickaxe, golden sword, lava bucket, compass) in a new world while baselines failed within 50 iterations; giving Voyager's skill library to AutoGPT improved AutoGPT. Released libraries hold ~57 skills per trial. Ablations: self-verification is the most important feedback (−73% items without it), automatic vs random curriculum −93%, GPT-3.5 code generation 5.7x fewer items.
limitations: Stated by authors: GPT-4 API cost (GPT-3.5 unusable); imprecise skills — agent still gets stuck, self-verification sometimes misjudges (e.g., not recognizing string as evidence of killing a spider); hallucinations — curriculum proposes non-existent items (copper sword/chestplate), code uses invalid recipes or nonexistent functions; no visual perception (uses Mineflayer API state, not pixels); building/spatial tasks require human critic/curriculum (manual mode). Observed from code: skill library is append-only with silent overwrite on name collision and no re-validation; the critic never sees code or trajectory, only final state; all skill code is concatenated into the JS runtime every step; retrieval is by GPT-3.5 paraphrase with no usage/success statistics; difficulty is tuned by hardcoded heuristics (peaceful->easy after 15 tasks, hardcoded first task and chest tasks); evaluation is on one game with 3 seeds; repo pinned to 2023 gpt-4, langchain 0.0.x, chromadb<0.4, Minecraft 1.19 Fabric plus Azure login — hard to reproduce today.
key_insight: Make executable, composable code the unit of learned capability: store only environment-verified programs, index them by natural-language description embeddings for retrieval, and inject them back as callable helpers so new skills compose old ones — capability compounds without weight updates and without catastrophic forgetting, and the closed loop propose -> retrieve -> generate -> execute -> verify -> store is what turns an LLM into a lifelong learner.
safety_measures: Prompt-level constraints only (no infinite loops/recursion, no event listeners, maxDistance 32 'do not cheat', define variables inside functions); babel syntax parse before execution; max 4 rounds per task and 160-iteration cap; env request timeout (600s); on rollout exception the env is hard-reset restoring inventory/position; optional revert of placed blocks on failed tasks (reset_placed_if_failed); optional 'manual' modes where a human replaces the curriculum or critic. No sandboxing of generated JS beyond the Mineflayer Node process, no rollback of skill-library writes, no human approval by default.
open_gaps: Skill library is append-only: no fitness/usage/success-rate tracking, no pruning, no re-validation of a skill after the world state it was born in changes
Name collision silently overwrites a skill (skill.py add_new_skill) with no regression test on skills that compose the old version — no versioning semantics or rollback
No refinement of existing skills: when a retrieved skill fails inside a new composition the fix is written as new code, never propagated back to the faulty skill

Verifier sees only final inventory/state, never the code or trajectory; the curriculum prompt explicitly forbids tasks the verifier cannot check (build/place/plant/trade), so the task space is shaped by verifier weakness
No held-out evaluation of stored skills; transfer is only measured in the same game with a new seed, no cross-domain or cross-API transfer
Single trajectory, single agent: no archive/population of alternative solutions, no explicit novelty or learning-progress metric — diversity relies on the prompt saying 'be novel'

Context budget is unmanaged: top-5 full skill source in the prompt and the entire library concatenated into the JS runtime each step; no hierarchical abstraction or summarization of skills as the library grows
Retrieval keyed only on a GPT-3.5 paraphrase of code; no preconditions/postconditions, dependency graph, or recency in ranking
Control primitives (mineBlock, craftItem, etc.) are hand-written and domain-specific; porting to another environment requires rewriting primitives and every prompt
Frontier-model dependency with no distillation: GPT-3.5 yields 5.7x fewer items and nothing is learned into weights or a cheaper model
Generated JavaScript runs unsandboxed inside the Mineflayer Node process; 'do not cheat' is a prompt instruction, not an enforced constraint
Reproducibility decay: pinned to 2023 gpt-4, langchain 0.0.x, chromadb<0.4, Minecraft 1.19 + Azure login; repo unmaintained since mid-2023

name: R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data
org_or_authors: Chengsong Huang, Wenhao Yu, Xiaoyang Wang, Hongming Zhang, Zongxia Li, Ruosen Li, Jiaxin Huang, Haitao Mi, Dong Yu — Tencent AI Seattle Lab, Washington University in St. Louis, UMD College Park, UT Dallas
last_activity: Repo last pushed 2026-02-04 (README typo fix); last substantive code change 2025-12-10; paper v4 2026-02-13
venue_or_citations: ICLR 2026 (accepted 2026-01-23); NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI workshop; HF Daily Papers #2 (2025-08-08). Citation count not retrievable (Semantic Scholar rate-limited); heavily cited by follow-ups Agent0, R-Few, VisPlay, Dr. Zero, Multi-Agent Evolve, Language Self-Play.
mechanism: One base LLM (Qwen3-4B/8B-Base, OctoThinker) is copied into two separately-trained weight sets: Challenger Q and Solver S. Each iteration (scripts/main.sh) has three phases. (1) Challenger GRPO, 5 steps: a single fixed prompt ("write one new competition-math problem, <question>…</question> + \boxed{answer}") is sampled n=4–5 times per group. Reward per question: the frozen current Solver (served via vLLM Flask servers) samples m=10 answers; p = fraction agreeing with the majority answer; r = min(p, 1−p) in code (paper: 1−2|p−0.5|, peak at p=0.5) minus a repetition penalty = share of the GRPO batch falling in the same BLEU agglomerative cluster (distance threshold 0.5); unparsable output gets −1. The Challenger's own \boxed answer is never used. (2) Data construction: trained Challenger samples 8×1000 = 8,000 questions at T=1.0; the Solver answers each 9–10 times; majority vote becomes the pseudo-label; keep only questions whose agreement lies in [0.3, 0.8] (paper δ=0.25, i.e. 3–7 of 10 agree); drop proofs/'text' answers; push to HF Hub as a dataset. (3) Solver GRPO, 15 steps (lr 1e-6, low-var KL coef 0.01, rollout n=5, rollout batch 512, 4096-token responses), binary reward = mathruler match to pseudo-label plus format check. Next iteration warm-starts both roles from their previous checkpoints; no reset, no population/archive, no rollback. Script loops 5 iterations; paper reports 3. Both weights AND the curriculum evolve, and because pseudo-labels come from the evolving Solver, the reward source co-evolves too.
eval_loop: Inside the loop there is NO external fitness signal: the Challenger is scored by Solver self-consistency (agreement with majority vote), and the Solver is scored by agreement with its own majority-vote pseudo-labels. Drift controls are only (a) the 0.3–0.8 agreement band, which drops questions that are trivially consistent or incoherent, (b) a BLEU-cluster repetition penalty within a GRPO batch (added after the authors observed near-duplicate question hacking, issue #8), (c) KL to the reference policy, and (d) fixed step counts (5/15) with no validation-gated checkpoint selection. Outer evaluation is post-hoc on external benchmarks after each Solver iteration: 7 math sets (MATH-500, GSM8K, AMC, Minerva, Olympiad, AIME24/25) scored rule-based then re-checked by GPT-4o (one-directional: only flips wrong to right), plus MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, BBEH. The paper's own GPT-4o oracle analysis shows the drift the loop cannot see: pseudo-label accuracy falls 79.0% (iter1) to 63.0% (iter3) as questions get harder, and performance collapses after 1 iteration for 0.6B and after 3 for 4B. Reproducers report (issue #20) 30–40% pseudo-label accuracy with the described protocol, and (issues #19/#31) the GPT-recheck script had swapped argument order; author concedes evaluation "had some issues" but says trends hold.
key_results: Qwen3-4B-Base: MATH avg 42.58 -> 49.07 (+6.49), overall avg 27.10 -> 34.92 (peak iter 2); Qwen3-8B-Base: MATH 49.18 -> 54.69 (+5.51), overall 34.49 -> 38.73, general-domain +5.13; OctoThinker-3B/8B also improve (+2.68 / +6.41 MATH). Zero-shot 'Base Challenger' (no RL) already gives ~half the gain (4B overall 30.83), RL-trained Challenger adds the rest. Ablations: removing Challenger RL training gives the largest drop; removing repetition penalty or difficulty filtering also hurts (exact numbers not retrievable here). R-Zero then SFT on human data beats SFT alone by +2.35 (4B). Single model playing both roles collapses earlier with lower pseudo-label accuracy. Gains saturate/decline by iteration 3; larger models tolerate more iterations.
limitations: Stated: pseudo-label accuracy degrades with difficulty (79%->63%); model collapse after 1–3 iterations; restricted to domains with single verifiable final answers (math); open-ended tasks unaddressed. Observed from code/issues: hyperparameters in paper and scripts disagree (batch 128 vs 16, steps 5/15 vs 6/20, m=10 vs 9); GPT-4o recheck bug and one-directional correction inflate absolute numbers (base Qwen3-4B MATH 58 rule-based vs 68 reported, Minerva ~20 vs 38); pseudo-label accuracy not reproducible (30–40% vs 79%); requires 8 GPUs, two full model copies, vLLM servers and HF Hub round-trips; pipeline is fragile (pkill python, math_verify infinite loops, hard-coded paths); tested only at 3B–8B; each iteration discards prior questions (no replay).
key_insight: Use the solver's own self-consistency as a single unified signal for three jobs at once: as the generator's reward (target p~0.5 = the solver's capability frontier), as the label (majority vote), and as the data filter (keep only the 0.3–0.8 band). This removes the need for any external verifier or seed data, but the same coupling is the failure mode: as the curriculum hardens, self-consistency stops tracking correctness and the loop drifts within ~3 iterations unless an external anchor is added.
open_gaps: No external correctness anchor: pseudo-labels are pure majority vote, accuracy drops 79%->63% in 3 iterations; a framework could add cheap verifiers (code execution, tool calls, cross-model agreement, or a few human examples as R-Few does) or weight training samples by label confidence

No stopping, checkpoint-selection, or rollback rule: fixed 5/15 GRPO steps and fixed iteration count, collapse is only detected post-hoc on external benchmarks; needs a held-out or synthetic validation gate that can reject an iteration and revert

Single lineage, no archive or population: each iteration overwrites both roles, previous 8k-question sets are discarded (no replay/curriculum memory); a quality-diversity archive of tasks and checkpoints would counter diversity collapse and length inflation documented by R-Few
Repetition penalty is only intra-batch BLEU clustering; no cross-iteration novelty measure, so the Challenger can re-converge on the same problem families over time

Domain locked to single-answer competition math via a hard-coded generator prompt; no mechanism for open-ended, multi-step, or tool-using tasks (Agent0/Dr. Zero extend this with tools and search) and no cross-domain task mixing
Requires full-parameter RL of two model copies on 8 GPUs plus vLLM reward servers; no LoRA/API/prompt-level variant, so app developers cannot use the loop with closed models
Challenger's own \boxed answer is generated then discarded; no self-verification of the generator's solution, wasted signal that could be used to detect ambiguous questions

Evaluation reproducibility is weak (swapped-argument GPT recheck, one-directional correction, paper/script hyperparameter mismatches); a new framework should report rule-based and judge-based scores separately and pin the exact loop config
Single shared-parameter model for both roles collapses earlier and the paper offers no fix; role separation via LoRA adapters or role tokens is untested
Generalization is measured only after the fact on math and three general benchmarks; the loop has no internal signal about transfer, so it cannot steer toward skills that generalize
safety_measures: Minimal and all internal to training: KL regularization to reference policy; BLEU-cluster repetition penalty against duplicate-question reward hacking; 0.3–0.8 agreement band filter; proof/'text'-answer exclusion; 10s grader timeouts. No sandboxing concerns (no code execution), no human-in-the-loop, no rollback, no drift detection during the run. Ethical/safety discussion absent from paper; model collapse is treated as a scientific finding, not an operational safeguard.

name: Self-Improvements in Modern Agentic Systems: A Survey
org_or_authors: Zhe Ren, Yimeng Chen, Dandan Guo, Guowei Rong, Tonghui Li, R.B. Xiong, Qingfeng Lan, Wenyi Wang, Li Nanbo, Yibo Yang, Mingchen Zhuge, Jürgen Schmidhuber — Jilin University, KAUST, University of Alberta, IDSIA/USI/SUPSI
last_activity: 2026-09-11 (companion awesome-list repo still receiving PRs; paper v1 July 2026)
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint (COLM-style template, no accepted venue found); Semantic Scholar: 9 citations / 1 influential (as of 2026-09-11); HF Daily Papers 35 upvotes; ~521 cited works
mechanism: This is a survey, so the 'loop' is a formalism rather than a running system. Agent configuration A_t = (theta_t, Sigma_t): theta = frozen-or-trainable FM weights; Sigma = (p, m, T, g) = prompts, memory + read/write policy, tools + invocation schemas, control logic (routing/scheduling/safety). Transient execution state X_t (KV cache, dialogue history, working memory) is explicitly excluded — only durable commits to theta or Sigma count as self-improvement. Self-improvement is one self-induced update operator: A_{t+1} = U(A_{1:t}, E(pi_{theta,Sigma}; Sigma_t, C_t)), where E is the agent executing its own policy in a task context C_t to emit a signal S_t (trajectories, critiques, preference pairs, verifier results, proposed edits) and U commits it. Sigma_t is passed into E so the agent can self-inspect its own scaffold. Two modes: (1) indirect/distributional — agent generates data/rewards consumed by an external optimizer (SFT/DPO/RL) on theta, the 'slow loop'; (2) direct/action-level — agent edits p/m/T/g itself, the 'fast loop' (cheap, reversible, inspectable). Full-scaffolding updates are modeled as the agent-as-improver executing on its own serialized program: candidate = exec(<Sigma_t>; S_t), materialized as patch Delta_t, committed only if verifier V(Sigma_t + Delta_t) = 1, else rollback to Sigma_t; the improver I_{Sigma_t} lives inside Sigma_t so it evolves with what it improves (Gödel-machine lineage). A 'skill' is defined as a serialized, reusable instance of U stored in any substrate; meta-level skills (write a tool, refactor a prompt, patch own scaffold) make the operator part of its own operand. History theta_{1:t}/Sigma_{1:t} is kept for validation and rollback.
eval_loop: Survey prescribes rather than runs an eval loop. Recommended protocol: track trajectory m_t = E[Phi(x, tau)] over iterations under a cumulative budget b_t <= B_max on a held-out D_eval (hidden or post-cutoff tasks), with explicit checkpoints, acceptance criteria and early stopping. Phi is either metric-based (executable unit tests, deterministic) or judge-based (LLM/Agent-as-a-Judge with rubric kappa). Anti-drift / anti-reward-hacking measures: (a) evaluator independence — use a different judge model/rubric for reporting than for driving updates; (b) the critic is 'governed infrastructure': decouple proposer from acceptor, allow the critic to evolve only monotonically (additive test generation) and gate its changes behind human audit; (c) verifier-gated commit of every structural patch (functional correctness, tool-permission boundaries, robustness to random state perturbation); (d) report regression rate on previously-solved tasks, tail-risk and safety violations per iteration, multi-seed variance, and full cost breakdown incl. quantified human input. Fast scaffold loop is where noisy feedback should be absorbed; parametric consolidation deferred until behavior is stable, then re-run adversarial safety tests because any theta update invalidates prior safety bounds.
key_results: No experiments — survey/position paper. Contributions: (1) unified formalism A=(theta,Sigma), Sigma=(p,m,T,g), self-improvement as update operator U with execution operator E; (2) two-axis taxonomy: FM improvement by signal type (intrinsic generative demonstrations D_t, intrinsic evaluative feedback e_t, extrinsic exploratory experience tau_t incl. grounded vs simulated envs) and scaffolding improvement by component (prompt: scalar-feedback / qualitative-feedback / population-based / textual-gradient; memory: object / structure / CRUD processing loop; tool: routing / refinement / creation; full scaffolding: ADAS, STOP, Gödel Agent, DGM, HGM, AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, Live-SWE-Agent, Agent Symbolic Learning); (3) 'skill' formalized as reusable serialized update operator orthogonal to substrate; (4) evaluation protocol with 6 required reporting items and a paper-benchmark incidence matrix across 6 domains; (5) three design principles (fast exploration -> slow consolidation; critic as governed infrastructure; layered gating / agent as untrusted code) and six future directions. ~521 cited works, ~28k words. Companion awesome-list repo: 471 stars, 49 forks, active PRs.
limitations: Purely descriptive: no algorithm, code, benchmark or empirical comparison; the operator U is a notational wrapper around heterogeneous methods, not a computable procedure. Formalism holds one of theta/Sigma fixed per step — joint theta+Sigma optimization and cross-substrate credit assignment are explicitly deferred to future work. The verifier gate V is only written down for full-scaffolding updates; memory/prompt/tool commits have no stated acceptance semantics. 'Skill' definition is loose (anything retained and reused). Safety guidance (monotone critics, human audit, layered gating) is qualitative with no threat model or protocol. Evaluation section is a checklist, not a harness. Taxonomy overlaps heavily with Gao et al. 2025 / Fang et al. 2025 self-evolving-agent surveys (the paper's own comparison table shows mostly 'secondary vs primary' differences). Strong Schmidhuber-lineage framing (Gödel machine, success-story algorithm) may overweight that lineage. Only 9 citations after ~2 months.
key_insight: Treat the agent as (frozen weights, serializable scaffold Sigma=(prompts, memory, tools, control logic)) and treat every form of self-improvement — from DPO on weights to a coding agent patching its own harness — as one verifier-gated, self-induced update operator whose signal comes from the agent's own execution; do noisy, reversible adaptation in the scaffold fast loop and only consolidate into weights once behavior is proven stable, and keep the critic outside the agent's unconstrained control.
open_gaps: No reference implementation of Sigma=(p,m,T,g) as typed, versioned substrates with a single generic gated commit/rollback API — a framework could ship this directly
Joint theta+Sigma optimization with cross-substrate credit assignment (decide per failure whether to edit a prompt, rewrite a tool wrapper, write memory, or fine-tune) is explicitly unsolved

Verifier gate V is only specified for full-scaffold patches; no acceptance criteria or regression checks are defined for memory writes, prompt edits, or tool additions, leaving memory poisoning and prompt drift persisting across sessions

No concrete protocol for safely evolving the critic/evaluator beyond 'additive test generation + human audit' — no mechanism to detect proposer/acceptor collusion or judge over-optimization automatically

The recommended evaluation protocol (trajectory under budget, held-out transfer, regression rate, cost breakdown, quantified human input) exists only as a checklist; no standardized self-improvement benchmark harness implements it, and the paper's incidence matrix shows methods evaluate on disjoint benchmarks
No non-stationary testbeds (drifting APIs, UI redesigns, adversarial users) for measuring whether self-improvement survives open-world distribution shift
Resource-aware improvement (cheap invariant checks gating expensive LLM/judge evaluations, penalizing wasted iterations, budgeted exploration) has no proposed method
Test-time continual adaptation that patches retrieval/routing/memory on the fly without eroding global performance is named but not addressed
Multi-agent cooperative co-evolution via shared artifact repositories (regression tests, patches, tool wrappers) lacks any version-control or trust protocol
No standard serialization/portability format for 'installer-like' meta-level skills so that an update discovered by one agent can be applied to another agent or session
safety_measures: Prescriptive only: treat self-improving agent as untrusted code in a protected runtime; layered gating / strict permission system for self-modification; every structural patch must pass verifier checks (functional correctness, tool-permission boundaries, robustness to random state perturbation) before commit to Sigma_{t+1} or theta_{t+1}; decouple critic from generator; evolving critics restricted to monotone (additive) changes and gated by human audit trails; keep parameter/scaffold history for rollback; re-run adversarial safety testing after any weight update; track regression rates, tail risk and safety violations per iteration; flags full-scaffolding regime as highest risk because one-off prompt injections can become persistent architectural vulnerabilities (poisoned memory, hijacked tool logic). Cites Vingean reflection problem (weaker system reasoning about stronger successor) as unsolved.

name: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement (Lil'Log)
last_activity: 2026-07-04 (single publication; no updates observed)
org_or_authors: Lilian Weng (independent; ex-OpenAI, Thinking Machines Lab)
venue_or_citations: Self-published on Lil'Log; ~31-min read; 39 references. Downstream: one reading list explicitly built around it (leezythu/Awesome-Harness-Self-Improvement, created 2026-07-08, 85 stars). The large 'awesome-harness-engineering' lists (4k stars) predate the essay (March 2026) and do not cite it. Scout's 'DeepSeek endorsement' claim could not be verified (search budget exhausted).
mechanism: The essay is a survey/position piece; it does not run a loop itself. It defines a harness as 'the system surrounding a base model that orchestrates execution and decides how the model thinks and plans, calls tools and acts, perceives and manages context, stores artifacts, and evaluates results', and argues near-term RSI will start by optimizing this layer, not weights. It organizes the field on an 'optimization ladder' of what is mutated: instruction prompts -> structured context (ACE playbook bullets; MCE bi-level skill/context) -> workflow graphs (ADAS archive + meta-agent; AFlow MCTS over LLM-node graphs) -> harness code (Meta-Harness proposer coding agent keeping a Pareto frontier; DGM self-modifying agent with performance-weighted parent selection; Self-Harness; AHE) -> optimizer code (STOP improver improving itself via meta-utility; Promptbreeder's evolving mutation prompts). The canonical loop she distills: (1) run harness h_t on tasks, persist traces as files; (2) mine failures into verifier-grounded patterns mapped to a specific editable component (AHE's 7: system prompt, tool description, tool implementation, middleware, skill, sub-agent config, memory); (3) same or stronger model proposes bounded, diverse edits conditioned on editable surfaces, failure patterns, passing behaviors to preserve, and prior-edit summaries, each paired with a falsifiable predicted impact; (4) validate on held-in and held-out splits, accept only zero-regression candidates, log rejects; (5) merge to h_{t+1}, repeat. Joint harness+weight loops (SIA, Continual Harness) are noted as provisional.
eval_loop: Signal is always an external, verifier-grounded task score: Terminal-Bench-2 / SWE-bench Verified / Polyglot pass rates, AFlow/ADAS task accuracy, STOP's meta-utility (mean utility of the improver across a task distribution), MCE's train/val split (inner loop on train, outer on val). Anti-drift measures she highlights from cited work: Self-Harness accepts an edit only if there is no regression on both held-in and held-out splits; AHE makes the runs directory, tracer, verifier and LLM config read-only so gains are attributable to harness edits and the loop cannot disable the verifier, swap models or raise reasoning budgets; AHE also requires each edit to carry a falsifiable prediction checked next round, and tests transfer by freezing the evolved harness and running SWE-bench Verified; ShinkaEvolve rejects candidates too similar to the population via embedding cosine similarity; DGM/ADAS keep an archive and only re-admit candidates above a threshold. Her stated principle: the evaluator and permission control must sit outside the evolving loop, with held-out tests, trace audits and human review at decision points. Weak/fuzzy evaluators (research taste, novelty, long-term repo health) are named as the primary unsolved bottleneck.
key_results: No new experiments (synthesis only). Numbers she relays: DGM raised Claude 3.5 Sonnet from 20% to 50% on SWE-bench Verified and 14.2% to 30.7% on Polyglot; AHE beats OpenCode/Terminus-2/Codex on Terminal-Bench-2 except the Hard tier and transfers frozen to SWE-bench Verified; Meta-Harness improves on Terminus-KIRA/Terminus-2 initializations; STOP improves with GPT-4 but degrades with GPT-3.5/Mixtral; Lin et al. 2026 find harness-updating ability is flat from Qwen3.5-9B to Claude Opus 4.6 while harness-benefit is non-monotonic (mid-tier models gain most); Trehan & Chopra's 6 auto-research failure modes; benchmark appendix (PaperBench ~21% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, CORE-Bench 21%, MLE-bench 16.9% bronze, RE-Bench humans win at 8-32h).
limitations: It is an essay, not a framework: no code, no unified interface, no new evidence; predictions ('harness improvements will be internalized into the model') are unfalsified. Almost all cited wins are on coding benchmarks with cheap exact verifiers; she concedes evolutionary methods 'struggle with domains where evaluation is slow, ambiguous, or mostly heuristic-based'. Recursive structure alone does not help weak models (STOP), and harness benefit is non-monotonic in model size, so results do not transfer across base models. SIA (joint weights+harness) is called 'provisional' due to confounded baselines. Reception claims in the scout note are overstated: the 'harness engineering' wave and its 4k-star lists predate the essay; only one 85-star list is derived from it.
key_insight: Because a harness is code, harness design becomes an executable search space that a coding agent can explore with the same tools human engineers use; the transferable recipe is: expose every editable component as a file, mine failures into component-attributed patterns, propose bounded edits paired with falsifiable predictions, and accept only on zero regression across held-in and held-out splits, with the evaluator and permission layer kept read-only outside the loop.
safety_measures: Prescribed rather than implemented: evaluator and permission control outside the evolution loop; explicitly declared editable surfaces (AlphaEvolve EVOLVE-BLOCK markers, AHE harness-workspace-only edits with read-only verifier/runs/model config); held-out regression gates before merging; trace audits; human review 'at the right time and abstraction level'; she flags that letting a program edit its own OS-like layer breaks abstraction boundaries and that all reward-hacking risks remain.
open_gaps: No reference implementation of the full ladder: ACE, MCE, Meta-Harness, Self-Harness, AHE and DGM each use bespoke file layouts and loops; a framework could define one component schema (system prompt, tool description, tool impl, middleware, skill, sub-agent config, memory) with a common editable-surface manifest and a pluggable proposer/validator.

Evaluator is fixed by fiat: the essay says the verifier must sit outside the loop but offers no mechanism to harden or extend evaluators for fuzzy domains (research taste, maintainability); a framework could evolve evaluators on a separate, human-audited track with disagreement detection against held-out labels.

No standard generalization gate: only AHE tests frozen-harness transfer to a second benchmark; acceptance criteria could require cross-benchmark or cross-task held-out gains, not just no-regression on the same suite.

Harness edits are not model-conditioned despite non-monotonic harness-benefit: a framework could measure harness-updating and harness-benefit separately per base model and gate or re-target edits by that profile.
Rejected edits are logged (Self-Harness) but never used: no system feeds the negative-result archive back into proposal conditioning to avoid repeated dead ends.
Diversity control is limited to embedding cosine rejection (ShinkaEvolve) on solution code; there is no diversity metric or niching for harness prompts/workflows to prevent population collapse.

Fitness is single-run task pass rate; long-horizon costs (repo health, backward compatibility, token/latency cost of the harness itself) are not in the objective; a framework could add multi-objective fitness with cost and maintainability terms.

Human touchpoints are unspecified: no concrete interface for which edits require approval, how to summarize a proposed edit plus its predicted impact for review, or how to feed human verdicts back as training signal.
Sample efficiency: every candidate needs full benchmark rollouts; no staged evaluation, early stopping, or bandit allocation across candidates is proposed beyond ShinkaEvolve parent sampling.
Joint harness+weights decision (SIA Feedback-Agent) is unvalidated; no clean protocol for when a recurring failure should trigger a weight update versus a harness edit.

name: ACE — Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models
org_or_authors: Qizheng Zhang, Changran Hu, Shubhangi Upasani, Boyuan Ma, Fenglu Hong, Vamsidhar Kamanuru, Jay Rainton, Chen Wu, Mengmeng Ji, Hanchen Li, Urmish Thakker, James Zou, Kunle Olukotun — Stanford University, SambaNova Systems, UC Berkeley
last_activity: Official code repo ace-agent/ace last pushed 2026-08-24 (ComBEE batched-curator merge); ace-appworld pushed 2026-07-24; paper v3 2026-03-29
venue_or_citations: arXiv 2510.04618 (cs.LG/cs.AI/cs.CL); third-party paper-notes list it as ICLR 2026 (not directly verified — arxiv/openreview unreachable from this machine). Semantic Scholar API rate-limited; by all indications several hundred citations and it is the default citation for playbook/memory-style self-improvement without weight updates. Official repo 1,310 stars / 168 forks; >20 independent reimplementations on GitHub.
mechanism:
The evolving artifact is a text "playbook": a sectioned list of bullets, each formatted `[slug-00042] helpful=X harmful=Y :: content`. Three LLM roles (paper: all non-thinking DeepSeek-V3.1) run per training sample:
1) Generator answers the task with the full playbook in context and must cite the bullet IDs it relied on.
2) Correctness is checked (ground-truth match for FiNER/Formula; AppWorld unit-test/execution feedback; a no-GT variant uses only execution feedback). Reflector receives trajectory + feedback + the cited bullets, writes a diagnosis/lesson, and tags each cited bullet helpful/harmful/neutral; counters are incremented deterministically (non-LLM). On failure, reflection→regeneration repeats up to max_num_rounds (3 in code, 5 in paper).
3) Curator sees playbook + stats + reflection and emits JSON delta operations; a deterministic merge appends new bullets with fresh IDs (C_{t+1} = C_t ∪ δ_t). No full rewrite ever happens — this is the anti-collapse guarantee.
4) Optional grow-and-refine: BulletpointAnalyzer embeds bullets (all-mpnet-base-v2 + FAISS), groups pairs with cosine ≥0.9, and LLM-merges each group, summing counters. Off by default.
Offline mode: iterate over a train split for N epochs (paper: up to 5), evaluate on a val split every eval_steps and keep best_playbook by val accuracy; the result is used as a fixed system prompt. Online mode: same loop over the test stream (batch size 1), the playbook acts as test-time memory. A 2026 "ComBEE" batched mode runs generator+reflector in parallel per mini-batch, each proposing ADDs from the same snapshot, then an LLM reducer dedups proposals before one merge. Single-lineage, no population or archive.
eval_loop: Signal = per-sample task correctness (exact/normalized match vs. ground truth on FiNER/XBRL-Formula; AppWorld TGC/SGC from the environment's unit tests, or raw execution feedback in the no-GT variant) plus an LLM-judge Reflector that attributes credit/blame to individual cited bullets (helpful/harmful counters). Anti-drift measures: (a) delta-only, deterministic merges so knowledge cannot be silently compressed (the failure they measured in Dynamic Cheatsheet: 18,282-token context → 122 tokens at step 61, accuracy 66.7→57.1, below the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline); (b) offline mode checkpoints best_playbook by held-out validation accuracy, so a degrading playbook is not shipped; (c) curator output is JSON-schema validated and skipped on failure. There is no reward-hacking guard beyond this: counters are recorded but never used to prune in released code, online mode has no rollback, and an issue reports val accuracy oscillating 93%→53% across epochs as the playbook bloats.
key_results: AppWorld (DeepSeek-V3.1 ReAct; TGC test-normal / TGC test-challenge / avg of TGC+SGC): ReAct base 63.7/41.5/42.4; +ICL 64.3/46.0/46.0; +MIPROv2 ~37.7 avg; +GEPA 64.9/46.0/46.4; +ACE offline 76.2/57.3/59.4 (+17.1 over base); +ACE offline no-GT 75.0/54.4/57.2; online: +Dynamic Cheatsheet 65.5/52.3/51.9 vs +ACE online 69.6/66.0/59.5. Leaderboard snapshot 2025-09-20: ReAct+ACE 59.4 vs IBM-CUGA (GPT-4.1) 60.3 average, ACE ahead on test-challenge. Finance (FiNER / Formula / avg): base 70.7/67.5/69.1; GEPA 73.5/71.5/72.5; ACE offline 78.3/85.5/81.9; ACE offline no-GT ~71.1/83.0/77.1; ACE online 76.7/76.5/76.6. Headline "+10.6% agents, +8.6% finance" are averages over baselines/settings. Cost: offline AppWorld −82.3% adaptation latency and −75.1% rollouts vs GEPA; online FiNER −91.5% latency and −83.6% token cost vs Dynamic Cheatsheet (86.9% average latency reduction). Ablations (AppWorld offline avg): w/o Reflector & multi-epoch ≈55.1, w/o multi-epoch ≈56.8, full 59.4; online without offline warmup 56.1 vs 59.5 with. v3 (Mar 2026) reportedly adds medical (DDXPlus), text-to-SQL (BIRD) and Gemini-model results (not verified first-hand). Independent user report (repo issue #26, Gemini 2.0 Flash, lending compliance): +8% test after 3 epochs.
limitations: Stated: heavily dependent on Reflector quality and on reliable feedback; noisy feedback can distil wrong lessons; long-horizon tasks may need hierarchical organisation; no-GT variant is clearly weaker on knowledge-intensive finance (FiNER 71.1 vs 78.3). Observed/skeptical: (1) released code implements ADD only — UPDATE/MERGE/DELETE are TODO stubs and the curator prompt only offers ADD, so the paper's "pruning of harmful bullets" is not what the code does; playbooks grow unboundedly (>100K tokens within 300 FiNER samples, issue #11; released AppWorld playbooks are ~118–130KB) and the token_budget parameter is only shown to the LLM, never enforced. (2) All three roles use the same model; no study of cheaper reflector/curator. (3) Benchmarks are all verifiable, single-domain tasks with train/val/test splits — no cross-task or cross-domain transfer of a playbook is measured. (4) Online-mode results train on the test stream, so 'online' numbers include ordering effects that are not analysed. (5) Efficiency wins are relative to rewrite-heavy baselines (GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet), not to static retrieval. (6) The AppWorld 'with GT' trained playbook file in the release repo is empty (0 bytes), weakening the reproducibility story. (7) Helpful/harmful counters are collected but not acted on; the only regression control is offline best-checkpoint selection. 'Self-improving' is accurate for the context, but nothing else in the system (prompts of the three roles, merge logic, evaluator) evolves.
key_insight: Never let an LLM rewrite the whole memory: represent accumulated knowledge as append-only, individually addressable bullets with usage counters, have the model emit small deltas, and merge them deterministically — this structurally forbids context collapse and brevity bias while keeping the memory human-editable, and lets a small open model match GPT-4.1 production agents by accumulating detailed, domain-specific tactics instead of concise prompts.
open_gaps: No pruning/forgetting actually implemented: helpful/harmful counters are recorded but DELETE/MERGE/UPDATE are TODO stubs, so playbooks bloat past 100K tokens and validation accuracy oscillates across epochs — a framework needs counter-driven decay, budget enforcement and retrieval over the playbook

No rollback or A/B verification of individual deltas: a new bullet is merged without measuring whether it helps; only offline best-checkpoint-by-val-accuracy guards against regressions, and online mode has none

Fitness is a single in-distribution benchmark per playbook; no held-out generalisation or cross-task/cross-domain transfer of learned bullets is measured, and no mechanism exists to move playbooks between tasks or agents
Reflector credit assignment is an unverified LLM judgment on cited bullet IDs — no consistency checks, no multi-sample voting, no detection of wrong lessons or poisoned entries entering the playbook

Only the context evolves; the Generator/Reflector/Curator prompts, the bullet schema, the merge/dedup policy and the evaluator are fixed by hand (repo issue #37/#38 asks for per-dataset prompts) — a second-order loop that tunes these is absent
Single lineage, no population/archive: there is one playbook, no diversity, no branching or selection among alternative playbooks
Requires a labelled train/val split or a verifiable environment; no strategy for open-ended or subjective tasks where feedback is sparse or noisy
Sequential per-sample loop with three LLM calls plus reflection rounds per sample; parallel ComBEE mode only landed Aug 2026 and lacks reported numbers
Playbook is injected whole into context every call; no retrieval/selection of relevant bullets (roadmap item, unimplemented), so cost scales linearly with accumulated knowledge
safety_measures: Minimal. Bullets are human-readable with IDs, enabling manual inspection and "selective unlearning" (delete a bullet) — the paper's main safety argument. Curator output is JSON-validated and the step is skipped on malformed output. Offline mode retains the best playbook by validation accuracy rather than the final one. No automatic rollback, no sandboxing concerns (context-only, no code self-modification), no defence against incorrect or adversarial lessons being accumulated, and the harmful counter is never used to remove content.
