name: ASI-Arch (AlphaGo Moment for Model Architecture Discovery)
org_or_authors: Yixiu Liu, Yang Nan, Weixian Xu, Xiangkun Hu, Lyumanshan Ye, Zhen Qin, Pengfei Liu — GAIR / SII / Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Taptap
last_activity: Repo last push 2025-12-03 (file upload only); last substantive code commit 2025-08-04; no paper revision since v1.
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint only (not peer-reviewed). Semantic Scholar 2026-09-11: 21 citations, 0 influential. GitHub: 1,187 stars, 218 forks, 5 open issues.
mechanism:
The evolving artifact is a single PyTorch file (a DeltaNet-class linear-attention layer), not the agents. One experiment (pipeline.py) = sample -> evolve -> evaluate -> analyse -> update:

1. SAMPLE: candidate pool = top-50 archive entries by fitness. Parent drawn uniformly from ranks 1-10 (its code overwrites SOURCE_FILE); 4 references from ranks 11-50. Each entry's motivation/analysis/cognition are re-summarised by a low-temp LLM every cycle (never stored) to keep context non-static.
2. EVOLVE (Researcher, o3 + GPT-4.1): planner reads code, writes modified layer + motivation in one agent (to avoid design/implementation drift). Novelty gate: FAISS top-5 similar motivations -> LLM "repeated?" verdict; if repeated, re-plan with a dedup prompt. Sanity gate (o3 code checker): causal mask, sub-quadratic complexity, chunking, dynamic shapes; may rewrite; 10 retries.
3. EVALUATE (Engineer, GPT-4.1): trainer runs a bash script (20M params, 1B tokens, 2000 steps, FLAME + lm-eval with 500 samples/task). On failure a debugger agent patches the code from the error log, max 3 attempts. Paper also describes early-kill of runs 2-3x slower or with suspiciously low loss.
4. ANALYSE (Analyst, o3): gets results plus parent/grandparent/strongest siblings as a pseudo-ablation, writes a structured analysis; the identified shortcoming is the RAG query into a Cognition Base (~100 linear-attention papers, 1-3 distilled "cognitions" each); top-3 stored with the node.
5. UPDATE: node inserted into MongoDB with parent pointer (phylogenetic tree). Every 50 insertions (after a 200-experiment cold start with no updates) the pool is re-scored and truncated to 50. Fitness = sigmoid(Δloss vs DeltaNet, ±10% window) + sigmoid(Δbenchmark) + LLM-judge (1-10, DeltaNet=5, GatedDeltaNet=10; rubric weights performance 30%, innovation 25%, complexity/efficiency 45%). Loss >10% below baseline = leakage, discarded. Many workers share the DB in parallel.

Stage 2 (manual): 1,350 20M winners -> ~400 retrained at 340M/1B tokens -> 106 beat baselines -> 5 hand-picked trained on 15B tokens.
eval_loop: Signal = composite fitness per architecture: sigmoid-capped final-train-loss delta and sigmoid-capped average-benchmark delta vs a fixed DeltaNet baseline (only ±10% window counts), plus an LLM-as-judge score on a rubric anchored to DeltaNet=5/GatedDeltaNet=10. Selection is elitist: only top-50 pool members are ever parents. Anti-hacking measures: sigmoid capping so no single metric dominates; discard runs whose loss is >10% below baseline as information leakage; LLM code checker for causal-mask/complexity bugs; embedding+LLM novelty check to stop repeated ideas; batched pool updates and a 200-run cold start to keep diversity. Weaknesses: single seed, 500 samples per benchmark at 20M scale (noise floor unreported); one-third of fitness is a subjective judge whose largest weight (45% complexity/efficiency) is inferred from code, never measured; no held-out tasks; failed experiments are not archived (survivorship bias). Only ~8% of 20M winners survived the 340M re-check, showing the explore-stage fitness is a weak proxy. Final selection of 5 architectures and the 40 component categories were curated by humans.
key_results: 1,773 autonomous experiments at 20M params/1B tokens (~10k GPU-h); 1,350 beat DeltaNet on loss+benchmark at 20M; ~400 retrained at 340M/1B tokens (~10k GPU-h) of which 106 beat both DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet ("SOTA", Table 2: 7-task avg gains over GDN 42.10 range +0.27 to +2.48 pts; loss -0.007 to -0.077). Final 5 at 340M/15B tokens (Table 1, avg over 8 accuracy tasks): PathGateFusionNet 48.51, ContentSharpRouter 48.34, FusionGatedFIRNet 48.29, HierGateNet 48.24, AdaMultiPathGateNet 48.18 vs Mamba2 47.84, Gated DeltaNet 47.32, DeltaNet 46.54 (note their GDN reproduction underperforms Mamba2, unlike the GDN paper, hinting at under-tuned baselines; no seeds/variance reported). "Scaling law": cumulative SOTA count grows linearly with GPU-hours (Fig. 1), i.e., a constant hit-rate, not a Kaplan-style law. Pool fitness plateaus by design while raw loss/benchmark keep improving; parameter counts stay stable (no bloat). Provenance (LLM-classified): gallery ideas 44.8% experience/analysis, 48.6% cognition, 6.6% original vs 37.7/51.9/10.4 for non-gallery. Models: o3 (planner, checker, analyst), GPT-4.1 (planner mix, dedup, trainer, debugger).
limitations: Stated by authors: single initial architecture (DeltaNet) so all discoveries are DeltaNet variants; no ablation of pipeline components (cognition vs analysis vs judge); no custom kernels so efficiency/latency never measured despite being 45% of the judge rubric. Observed: gains are marginal (sub-1-point average at 15B tokens vs Mamba2) with single seed and no significance testing; benchmark evaluation uses 500 samples/task at 20M scale; the "ASI"/"AlphaGo moment"/"scaling law for discovery" framing far outruns the evidence; the released repo omits the training script (issue #10), config is placeholders, real-time anomaly termination is not in the code, and it hard-depends on Azure OpenAI o3/GPT-4.1, MongoDB, OpenSearch, FAISS, Docker plus ~20k GPU-hours; repo effectively dormant since Aug 2025 with install issues open; 21 citations/0 influential after 14 months. Agents themselves never change — "self-evolution" refers to the target artifact plus its archive, so this is AlphaEvolve-style evolutionary program search with an LLM judge, not a self-improving agent.
key_insight: Treat the archive's post-mortem analysis as a first-class evolvable memory: each child is analysed against its parent, grandparent and strongest siblings (a free pseudo-ablation), the identified shortcoming is used to retrieve distilled literature "cognitions", and both are stored on the node and fed to the next proposal — their provenance study claims the best designs lean more on this accumulated experience (44.8%) than the population average, i.e., evolving what the system knows about the search space matters as much as mutating the artifact. Secondary: sigmoid-capped deltas plus an LLM judge blunt single-metric reward hacking, and a cheap explore stage (20M) feeding an expensive verify stage (340M) is what made 1,773 trials affordable.
open_gaps: Fitness is single-seed, 500-sample-per-task at 20M params with no variance estimate or held-out task suite; only ~8% of 20M winners survived the 340M re-check, so the cheap proxy needs multi-seed/significance gating or a learned scale-transfer predictor before promotion.
The search procedure itself is frozen: planner prompts, judge rubric, dedup rules, and sampling policy never change in response to discovery yield — no meta-level self-improvement of the harness.

One-third of fitness is an uncalibrated LLM judge whose largest weight (45% complexity/efficiency) is inferred from code and never measured; no human-rating calibration or measured throughput/latency in the loop.
Failed or rejected experiments (evolution/eval failures) are not stored in the archive, so the memory has survivorship bias and the system cannot learn 'what not to try'.

Elitist top-50 scalar pool with no quality-diversity/niching (MAP-Elites style), so lineages collapsed onto gating/routing variants of one DeltaNet class; only 6.6% of gallery ideas judged 'original'.
Novelty check compares motivation text embeddings plus an LLM opinion, never code or behavioral equivalence; functionally identical architectures with different prose pass.
Hard-coded to a single DeltaNet class inside FLA/FLAME with a Delta-specific judge rubric; no abstraction for swapping the target artifact or task family (no cross-domain transfer).

Human intervention remains at key points: cold-start/threshold hyperparameters, choosing the 5 finalists for the 15B-token run, and curating 40 component categories — the 'fully autonomous' claim stops at stage 1.
No sandboxing or resource limits: agents rewrite a file and run a bash script via subprocess on shared GPUs; parallel workers share an unauthenticated MongoDB/REST API.
Not usable without ~20k GPU-hours, Azure OpenAI o3/GPT-4.1, MongoDB, OpenSearch, FAISS and Docker; training script and anomaly-monitoring code are not released, so end-to-end reproduction is blocked.
safety_measures: No dedicated safety section. Practical guards only: LLM code checker for causal-mask leakage and O(n^2) complexity; runs with loss >10% below baseline treated as information leakage and discarded; sigmoid capping of metric deltas to discourage single-metric hacking; bounded retries (10 for evolve/checker, 3 for debug); paper describes killing runs that are 2-3x slower or have abnormally low loss. No sandboxing (agents write code and execute a bash script via subprocess), no resource quotas, no authentication on the shared DB API, no rollback concept (the agent code never self-modifies).

name: Self-Evolving Coding Agents (survey)
org_or_authors: Hao Zhou, Haichuan Hu, Quanjun Zhang (Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Ye Shang (Nanjing University)
last_activity: 2026-08-29 (companion repo zhouhao1024/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Coding-Agents last push; paper still v1)
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint v1 only (2026-08-04), no venue / not peer-reviewed; citation count unavailable (Semantic Scholar rate-limited), 9 HuggingFace upvotes, 83 references, ~9.5k-word body, Table 2 classifies ~30 representative systems
mechanism: This is a survey, not a system; it contributes no loop of its own but a three-axis frame for describing loops in coding agents. Axis 1, the object of evolution (RQ1): (a) agent framework / scaffold rewriting and archive-based variant search (SICA, SIFT, STOP, DGM, Mendel GM, Huxley GM); (b) memory: experience banks, subtask-aligned memory, repository memory from commit history, vulnerability-repair experience (SWE-Exp, EvoCoder, Subtask Memory, RepoMemory, EvoRepair, SAGE); (c) skills and tools distilled from trajectories or learned per repository, plus on-the-fly tool synthesis (CODESKILL, gskill, Socratic-SWE, EffiSkill, Live-SWE-Agent); (d) model-side: policy/verifier updated from the agent's own verified attempts (Self-play SWE-RL, Agent-RLVR, ReVeal, CURE, ZeroCoder, Sol-Ver, ACE); (e) workflow and topology: mutable roles, DAGs, communication density (SEMAG, EvoMAC, SEW, AFlow, EvoAgentX, AgentConductor). The companion repo adds a sixth: environment/context (TACO, SWE-Pruner, EvoConfig). Axis 2, evolving time (RQ2): task-time (adapt within the current task), post-task (abstract a finished trajectory into memory/skills), stage-wise (batch trajectories into policy or agent-generation updates). Axis 3, evidence: outcome (solve rate, cost, verifier score = selection pressure), environmental feedback (compiler, tests, tool errors = in-task adaptation), trajectory-derived (full traces = memory/skill/curriculum distillation). The survey's sharpest definitional move is a closed-loop boundary: post-training counts as self-evolution only if the signal is generated by the agent's own attempts (so SWE-RL, SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-RM are classified as infrastructure or learned evidence, not self-evolving agents).
eval_loop: The survey runs no experiments and reports no numbers of its own. It catalogs the signals used by surveyed systems: outcome evidence (SWE-bench/Verified/Lite/Pro resolve rate, HumanEval/MBPP/APPS/CodeContests/LiveCodeBench pass rate, cost/runtime as in SICA, archive fitness as in DGM), environmental feedback (unit tests, compiler diagnostics, CI logs, sandboxed execution, adversarially generated tests in ACE/CURE), trajectory-derived evidence (traces distilled into experience banks or skill registries, LLM-judge rubrics in CODESKILL and SIFT), and learned verifiers/reward models (SWE-RM). On drift and reward hacking it is diagnostic only: it flags that benchmark-selected self-modifications are sensitive to evaluation noise and leakage, that a harness-modifying agent can exploit the evaluation harness, that self-play loops need learnable information gain per iteration (citing Liu et al. 2026) or they reinforce bias, and that memories/skills go stale or get contaminated by failed trajectories. It recommends validation, rollback, skill audits, and held-out transfer tests but specifies no concrete protocol.
limitations: Narrative synthesis with no quantitative meta-analysis, no reproduced results, no headline numbers, and no comparison table of reported gains; Table 2 covers only ~30 systems while the companion repo already lists 65 core papers (27 in the framework/harness category alone versus 6 discussed in the paper), so the text lags its own corpus; the taxonomy (what/when/evidence) is a domain specialization of prior general surveys (Gao et al. 2026, Fang et al. 2025) rather than a new lens; the safety/rollback/validation discussion stays at the level of exhortation with no mechanism catalog; product coverage (Claude Code memory, Cursor, Devin, Copilot) exists only in the repo README and is explicitly caveated as undocumented mechanisms; arXiv v1 only, not peer-reviewed, five weeks old; 'self-evolving' is used loosely for anything that persists state across tasks.
key_insight: Software engineering is the natural substrate for agent self-evolution because its feedback is executable and repeatable, but a loop only counts as self-evolution when the signal closes around the agent's own attempts; the same executable signals that make evolution cheap also propagate errors into persistent state (memory, skills, scaffold, weights), so validation, rollback and held-out transfer must be first-class parts of the loop, not afterthoughts.
key_results: No experimental results (survey). Structural outputs: three research questions; a five-category object-centered taxonomy (framework, memory, skill/tool, model, workflow/topology), extended to six in the repo (environment/context); a 3-way temporal typology (task-time / post-task / stage-wise); a 3-way evidence typology (outcome / environmental / trajectory-derived); a closed-loop boundary criterion excluding SWE-RL, SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-RM from 'self-evolving'; a challenges list (reproducibility and benchmark overfitting, feedback reliability and harness exploitation, stale memory/skills and coordination cost, evaluation beyond short benchmarks, no evidence of transfer to non-coding domains). Companion awesome-list: 174 entries, 139 stars, 11 forks, includes 27 harness-evolution papers (AHE, HarnessFix, TTHE, HarnessCompass, Evo-Harness, EvolveNet, HELIX, Ouroboros, HarnessBank, DarwinX, Self-Harness, Meta-Harness, HarnessX, etc.).
safety_measures: None proposed; the survey only names the need for validation, rollback, robustness checks, memory revision, skill audits, and constrained self-modification, and notes that framework-level evolution can break the agent loop or exploit the evaluation harness. It contains no threat model, no sandboxing guidance, and no catalog of how surveyed systems actually gate or revert self-modifications.
open_gaps: No system in the survey evolves more than one object at a time in a coordinated way (e.g. joint scaffold + skill + memory updates with shared attribution); a framework could unify the five/six objects under one mutation-and-selection loop
Rollback and verification of self-modifications are only called for, never specified: no surveyed system offers versioned scaffold state, regression gates, or automatic revert on held-out degradation

Fitness is almost always a single public benchmark (SWE-bench variants, HumanEval); no protocol for held-out repositories, contamination-aware task generation, or measuring generalization beyond the evolved setting

Memory and skill stores have no staleness, redundancy, or contamination controls; nothing surveyed retires memories/skills when repository state changes or when a stored lesson was learned from a flaky test
Evidence reliability is untreated: no surveyed loop weights signals by test coverage, flakiness, or verifier calibration, so misleading feedback propagates into persistent state
Transfer of evolved artifacts is only in-domain; no evidence that skills/scaffolds learned on one repo or language transfer to others or to non-coding tasks
No cost accounting or budget-aware evolution: repeated benchmark evaluation of candidates is expensive and the survey reports no cost-vs-gain tradeoffs

Product-side mechanisms (Claude Code, Cursor, Devin, Copilot memory) are undocumented; a framework that exposes an auditable evolution log would fill the gap between research prototypes and deployed tools
Long-horizon quality (maintainability, security, reviewability) is never used as an evolution signal; all loops optimize for test passing

name: Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS) / Meta Agent Search
org_or_authors: Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Jeff Clune — University of British Columbia, Vector Institute, Canada CIFAR AI Chair
last_activity: 2025-01-28 (last repo push; arXiv v1 2024-08-15, ICLR 2025 camera-ready early 2025)
venue_or_citations: ICLR 2025 (poster, OpenReview t9U3LW7JVX); Outstanding Paper, NeurIPS 2024 Open-World Agents workshop; Semantic Scholar: 312 citations, 45 influential (2026-09-11)
mechanism: Verified from ShengranHu/ADAS `_mmlu/search.py` + `mmlu_prompt.py`. The unit of evolution is a single Python `forward(self, taskInfo)` function that composes calls to a fixed primitive `LLMAgentBase(output_fields, name, role, temperature)` (base LLM hard-coded to gpt-3.5-turbo-0125). The meta agent (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) is prompted once per generation with: the framework/utility code, a domain description + one example question, the ENTIRE archive dumped as JSON (each entry = thought, name, code, fitness string), a list of "WRONG implementation" anti-patterns, and the instruction to "maximize fitness by proposing interestingly new agents... THINK OUTSIDE THE BOX". It returns {thought, name, code}. Two fixed reflection turns follow in the same chat: Reflexion_1 asks it to judge novelty vs the archive, find implementation bugs, and improve; Reflexion_2 re-applies the anti-pattern checklist. The code is then `exec()`'d in-process and run on a validation slice; if it throws or scores <1% ("All 0 accuracy"), the traceback is appended and the meta agent debugs, up to debug_max=3 times. Any agent that runs is appended to the archive with fitness = "median + 95% bootstrap CI" string — there is no improvement threshold, no parent selection, no pruning, no crossover; the archive is a flat chronological list. The archive is seeded with 7 hand-written baselines (CoT, CoT-SC, Self-Refine, LLM Debate, Step-back, QD, Role Assignment). Runs 25-30 generations, one candidate per generation, single-threaded search. After search, every archived agent is re-scored on a disjoint test slice. The meta agent, reflection prompts, evaluator, and base model never change.
eval_loop: Signal = ground-truth benchmark accuracy (F1 for DROP) of the exec'd forward() on a fixed validation slice: 128 questions (DROP/MGSM/MMLU), 32 questions x5 repeats (GPQA), small ARC subset x5 repeats; reported as median + 95% bootstrap CI string, which is the only feedback the meta agent sees (no per-example traces). No LLM judge. Drift/hacking controls: (1) the meta agent never sees validation questions (only one example) and answers are graded by exact match; (2) held-out test slice (800 questions) scored post hoc for every archived agent; (3) crash / <1% accuracy triggers debug retry rather than archiving. Weaknesses visible in the released `results/*.json`: fitness on 128 examples has a ~±8pp CI and val->test gaps up to 10pp (Self-Refine MMLU val 73.4 -> test 63.5); nothing is ever rejected for being worse than its predecessors, so the archive accumulates regressions (DROP gens 23-26 all scored ~10%); and the paper's headline numbers coincide exactly with the max TEST fitness over the archive, not the max VALIDATION fitness (see limitations).
key_results: All with GPT-3.5-turbo as the base model and GPT-4o as meta agent; numbers read directly from released archives and match the paper. Best-baseline test vs best-discovered test: DROP F1 65.8 -> 79.4 (+13.6); MGSM 39.0 -> 53.4 (+14.4); GPQA 31.6 -> 34.6; MMLU 65.9 -> 69.6; ARC 8.0 -> 13.7 (median over 5 runs). Paper-claimed transfer: MGSM-discovered agent gives +25.9 on GSM8K and +13.2 on GSM-Hard over baselines; agents found with GPT-3.5 keep their edge when swapped to Claude-Haiku, GPT-4, Claude-Sonnet (ARC ~50% on Sonnet per summaries); math agents transferred to DROP/MMLU/GPQA match or beat baselines. ICLR version adds an empty-archive ablation (no baseline seeds) that still beats hand-designed agents. Search trajectories are noisy, not monotone: MGSM's best agent appeared at generation 4 and was never exceeded in 26 further generations.
limitations: (1) Selection bias in headline numbers: the reported best agents are the archive entries with maximal TEST fitness; selecting by validation fitness (the only legitimate signal) gives DROP 70.7 (not 79.4), GPQA 32.3 (not 34.6), MMLU 69.1, ARC 10.7 — gains over baselines shrink to a few points and are within CI on GPQA/MMLU. (2) Fitness is a 128-example single-benchmark score with ±8pp CI; strong val/test disagreement. (3) No acceptance gate or pruning: every runnable candidate is archived, whole archive is dumped into the prompt each generation, so context grows linearly and search is capped at ~30 single-candidate generations. (4) Discovered agents are 10-50x more expensive than CoT (multi-candidate x multi-critic x multi-refinement loops); cost is not an objective. (5) `exec()` of model-written code in-process, no sandbox (README warns). (6) Base model fixed to gpt-3.5-turbo; only OpenAI models supported; repo abandoned since Jan 2025 with 11 open issues. (7) Meta agent, reflection prompts and evaluator are frozen — no meta-level self-improvement (later addressed by DGM / hyperagents). (8) Benchmarks are single-turn QA with exact-match grading; no tool-use, long-horizon or software tasks. "Self-evolving" is accurate for the agent code but the system as a whole is a fixed outer loop.
safety_measures: README warning that untrusted model-generated code is executed; paper discusses risk of self-improving systems and suggests future "safe-ADAS" incorporating Constitutional AI, and argues for transparency. In practice: no sandbox (plain exec with module globals), no network/IO restriction, no timeout, no human approval gate; the only guards are a context-length assertion and a <1%-accuracy rejection.
key_insight: Make the search space Turing-complete code (a forward() over a single FM-call primitive) and let an LLM meta-agent, conditioned on a growing archive of (design, fitness) pairs, write the next candidate — using the archive as stepping stones for in-context "reflection-driven" search rather than as a population under selection.
open_gaps: Select and report by validation fitness with a paired/held-out protocol; the current pipeline's headline numbers are best-of-archive on the test set
Variance-aware acceptance: 128-example fitness with ±8pp CI needs racing/successive-halving or paired bootstrap vs parent before an agent is archived or promoted

No regression gate or pruning: every runnable candidate is archived, so the archive accumulates collapsed agents (DROP gens 23-26 at ~10%) and the full archive is dumped into the prompt, capping search at ~30 generations
Single scalar fitness feedback: the meta agent never sees per-example failures or traces, so it cannot do credit assignment (contrast GEPA/ACE reflective traces)
No cost/latency objective or Pareto front; discovered agents are 10-50x more expensive than CoT (AFlow/EvoFlow later added this)
No sandboxing: exec() of LLM-written code in-process with module globals, network, and no timeout
Meta-level is frozen: the proposer prompt, reflection steps, debug loop and evaluator cannot be modified by the system (DGM/hyperagents gap)
No cross-domain reuse of discovered building blocks as a library; transfer is only tested post hoc by copying the single top agent
One candidate per generation, sequential; no parallel proposal, no crossover between archive entries, no lineage/tree structure
Only single-turn QA benchmarks with exact-match grading; no tool-use, multi-turn, or software-engineering tasks
Hard-coded to OpenAI gpt-3.5/4o via chat.completions JSON mode; repo unmaintained since 2025-01, not packaged for reuse by app developers

name: Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM)
org_or_authors: Wenyi Wang, Piotr Piękos, Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yimeng Chen, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Mingchen Zhuge, Jürgen Schmidhuber — KAUST (Center of Excellence for Generative AI); code at metauto-ai/HGM
last_activity: Repo last push 2026-02-07 (README news only); last code fix 2025-11-25; last substantive addition 2025-11-06 (best_agent + SWE-bench Lite results link)
venue_or_citations: ICLR 2026 Oral (OpenReview forum T0EiEuhOOL). Citation count not retrievable (Semantic Scholar rate-limited); ~20 tweets / 2 HN posts per EmergentMind; 431 stars / 71 forks; at least two independent reimplementations (weill-labs/hgm, z3nkr1s9n6-ctrl/hgm-lab); listed in coding-agent self-evolution surveys.
mechanism: Archive = a tree of coding-agent versions, each a git patch chain over a DGM-derived base agent (coding_agent.py forward() loop, tools/, prompts/). Budget = N benchmark task-evaluations (800 for the 60-task runs, 8000 for full SWE-bench Verified). Asynchronous loop with 20 workers; each iteration: if n_evals^α ≥ |tree| (+pending expansions), α=0.6 (UCB-Air widening rule), EXPAND, else EVALUATE. EXPAND: for every node with ≥1 success, pool the Bernoulli pass/fail outcomes of the node plus all its descendants (its clade) into (s_C, f_C); Thompson-sample Beta(τ(1+s_C), τ(1+f_C)) with τ=B/b annealing (config default: no annealing) and take the argmax. In a Docker container, apply the parent's patches, choose_entry picks one failed task (or a meta-issue: empty patches / stochasticity / context-length overflow), a diagnose LLM reads the agent's code, run log, the SWE-bench private test patch and eval log, and emits a general improvement plan; the parent agent is then run on its own repo (--self_improve) to implement it. A non-empty model_patch.diff becomes a child node with zero evaluations (no test gate; empty/failed patches are dropped). EVALUATE: Thompson-sample over nodes' own Beta(1+s, 1+f), give the winner one random not-yet-run task, run the official SWE-bench/Polyglot harness in Docker, append 0/1; counts propagate to all ancestors' clade tallies. At budget exhaustion return the best-belief agent (highest posterior percentile of per-agent Beta). Meta-level code (hgm.py, diagnosis/self-improvement prompts, the CMP estimator) is excluded from the container via .dockerignore, so only the object-level coding agent evolves.
eval_loop: Signal = binary resolved/unresolved from the official SWE-bench Verified (60-task DGM subset or full 500) or Polyglot harness, run in Docker with hidden tests; evaluation LLM is GPT-5-mini (SWE) / Qwen3-Coder-30B (Polyglot), expansion LLM GPT-5 / Qwen3-Coder-480B. Each outcome is a Bernoulli sample feeding Beta posteriors; clade-pooled posteriors (CMP estimate) drive which lineage to expand, per-agent posteriors drive which agent gets more evaluation, and the N^α ≥ |T| rule arbitrates expand-vs-evaluate. Drift/regression control is purely statistical: bad children accumulate failures and get deprioritized by Thompson sampling; there is no rollback, no unit-test gate on self-modifications, and no verification beyond downstream task sampling. Reward hacking is limited by the outer harness being outside the agent's editable repo and by Docker sandboxing, but the diagnosis step is shown the private SWE-bench test patch (train-subset leakage into the mutation operator). Generalization is checked once, post hoc, on SWE-bench Lite filtered to the 207 tasks not in Verified, and on a backbone swap to GPT-5.
key_results: SWE-Verified-60 (from 40.0% initial, 800 evals): HGM 56.7% vs DGM 53.3% vs SICA 50.0%; allocated CPU-hours 517 vs DGM 1231 (2.38x) vs SICA stuck in a context-length loop after 360 evals. Polyglot (from 20.3%): HGM 30.5% vs DGM 27.1% vs SICA 25.4%; 347 h vs 2385 h (6.86x) vs 572 h (1.65x). CMP-estimator vs empirical-CMP Pearson (weighted): HGM 0.778 / 0.626 vs DGM 0.285 / 0.383 vs SICA 0.444 / 0.274 (SWE / Polyglot). Full SWE-bench Verified with bash-only initial agent (53.2%) after 8000 evals: 61.4%, top GPT-5-mini system and top-10 among checked submissions. Transfer to SWE-bench Lite with GPT-5-mini: filtered (207 unseen) 40.1% vs ancestor 34.8% vs SWE-agent+GPT-5-mini 39.6%; standard 49.0% vs 44.0% vs 47.6%. Backbone swap to GPT-5: 57.0% (172/300, checked submission) vs SWE-agent+Claude 4 Sonnet 56.7%; filtered 47.8% vs 48.3%. Total spend for the three-method comparison ~$5000. Independent clean-room replication (weill-labs/hgm, May 2026): CMP beats greedy in a $0 simulator (+0.055 skill over 40 seeds); live it rescued a deliberately crippled agent (0.00→0.35 pass@1, p=0.016) but showed no net gain from a competent 0.26 base with 50 held-out instances (7–7 discordant pairs, p≈1.0).
limitations: Single run per method/benchmark, no seeds or confidence intervals; 56.7 vs 53.3 on 60 tasks is a 2-task difference. No ablation separating CMP from the other simultaneous changes vs DGM (async execution, single-task evaluation granularity, UCB-Air widening), so the paper cannot attribute the gain to the clade metric. The held-out advantage over the human-designed SWE-agent on unseen SWE-Lite tasks is ~0.5 pt (about one task). Empirical-CMP targets are computed on trees the policies themselves generated (policy-dependent confounding), with a hand-designed leakage correction. Theorem 1 (CMP oracle = Gödel Machine) is a Q-value identity under strong assumptions (repeatable trials, zero-cost proofs, unit-cost self-modifications, final-agent-only objective); no guarantees for the estimator, and the paper has no explicit limitations section. Async execution biases toward agents with few evaluations (acknowledged, unfixed). Cost is hundreds to thousands of CPU-hours plus ~$5k of LLM spend per comparison; requires Docker and the full SWE-bench harness. Config default cool_down=false diverges from the paper's τ=B/b schedule. Only the object-level agent is modified; the search policy and mutation prompts are fixed. API keys are injected into the sandbox running model-generated code.
key_insight: Score a candidate for further self-modification by the pooled downstream success of its entire lineage (clade) rather than its own benchmark score, and decouple 'spawn a child' from 'measure an existing node' so evaluation budget flows one task at a time to whichever node the posterior says is most promising — the parent's own fitness is a weak predictor of its descendants' fitness (Metaproductivity-Performance Mismatch).
open_gaps: Only the object-level coding agent (coding_agent.py, tools/, prompts/) is mutated; the self-improvement machinery itself (search policy, CMP estimator, diagnose and self-improve prompts, choose_entry heuristics) is explicitly excluded from the sandbox via .dockerignore — no meta-level self-improvement despite the Gödel Machine framing

Fitness is binary pass/fail on a fixed subset of one public benchmark (60 or 500 SWE-bench tasks); no held-out validation inside the loop, no task heterogeneity/difficulty modeling, no curriculum or task generation

No verification or rollback of self-modifications: a child enters the archive on any non-empty diff with no unit-test/static/diff-review gate; regressions are only discovered by spending benchmark evaluations on them

The diagnosis LLM is shown the SWE-bench private test patch and hidden-test logs of the training subset, leaking test knowledge into the mutation operator; a framework should isolate the mutator from held-out test contents

No statistical rigor or replication protocol: single run per configuration, no seeds/CIs, no ablation isolating CMP from async execution, single-task evaluation granularity, and the UCB-Air widening rule; an independent replication found a null effect from a competent base at small scale

Each expansion sees only its parent's code plus one diagnosed failure; there is no cross-lineage transfer, crossover, or persistent memory of which self-modifications worked, so discoveries in one clade are never reused by another

Compute cost is prohibitive for practitioners: 347–2385 allocated CPU-hours per run, 8000 evaluations for the full-benchmark run, ~$5k for the comparison; no cheap proxy or simulator for the search loop is provided (a third-party clean-room repo added one)
Asynchronous execution creates a known bias toward under-evaluated agents (easy tasks finish first, inflating early means); acknowledged but not corrected

Safety is Docker sandboxing plus a README warning; API keys are passed into the container environment of the self-modifying agent, and there is no monitoring of what the agent does to its own repo (e.g., the mutated agent could edit its internal eval_utils)

Theorem 1's assumptions (repeatable trials, zero-cost proofs, unit-cost modifications, final-agent-only objective) do not hold for real deployments where evaluation is noisy, costly, and non-stationary; no guarantees for the CMP estimator's bias or sample complexity are given
safety_measures: Every self-modification and every task evaluation runs inside a Docker container built from the initial-agent image; 1-hour (5-hour in Sec. 4.3) timeouts on self-modification and evaluation; the outer harness and search code live outside the agent's editable repo; README warns that model-generated code may behave destructively and asks users to accept the risk. No formal proofs (the 'Gödel Machine' link is a theoretical identity, not enforced at runtime), no rollback, no diff review, no unit-test gate on children; API keys (OpenAI/Anthropic/AWS/OpenRouter) are injected as environment variables into the sandbox running self-modification.

name: Your Agent May Misevolve: Emergent Risks in Self-evolving LLM Agents (Misevolution)
mechanism: This is NOT a self-evolution framework; it instruments four existing evolution loops and measures safety before vs. after, with safety never part of the objective. Formalization: agent θ=(model, memory, tools, workflow), θ'=f(θ, trajectory, feedback), f chosen to maximize cumulative task utility only. (1) Model: released checkpoints of Absolute-Zero (Qwen2.5-7B/14B Base/Coder self-proposes coding tasks; reward = learnability + Python-verified correctness; RL updates weights), AgentGen (Llama3.1-70B trained on self-generated environments/tasks), SEAgent (UI-TARS-7B, failure-driven curriculum), plus a 200-step AZR rerun probed on HarmBench every 10 steps. (2) Memory: SE-Agent (Qwen3-Coder-480B) evolves 3 rounds on SWE-Bench-Verified distilling strategies into context; AgentNet-style memory injected as 6 hand-written experiences (3 success/3 fail with satisfaction scores + success-rate table) over 40 cases in Sales/Service/Medical/Finance; a 'dynamic' variant runs a 100-round customer-agent -> service-agent -> evaluator-agent loop (all Qwen2.5-72B) writing scores+feedback back into memory. (3) Tools: Alita-style plan-and-act agent creates Python 'MCP' tools during a benign task ('creating helpful tools will be rewarded'), stores them in mcp_tools.jsonl, retrieves top-3/top-5 by bge-m3 embedding for a second security-sensitive task (25 CWEval-derived pairs); separately 371 GitHub repos with RedCode-Exec payloads injected are gitingest-ed and the agent decides whether to wrap them as MCPs. (4) Workflow: verbatim AFlow MCTS (optimizer LLM proposes graph+prompt modification, parent soft-selected from top-k rounds by validation score, 20 iterations on HumanEval, Qwen2.5-72B executor); best workflow then run on RedCode-Gen. Acceptance signal in every loop is utility only; no safety gate, no rollback.
eval_loop: Evolution in all studied systems is driven purely by task utility: AZR learnability/correctness rewards, SWE-Bench resolution, user-satisfaction scores from an evaluator agent, HumanEval pass rate for AFlow's MCTS selection, 'helpful tools rewarded' prompt. Safety is measured only externally by the authors: HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls, ShieldAgent (Agent-SafetyBench, 2000 cases), GPT-4o judge + rule-based (RiOSWorld UIR/UCR), Refusal Rate/ASR on RedCode-Gen (160 malware prompts, 8 categories), Gemini-2.5-Pro LLM judge plus human judge for reward-hacking and tool-reuse trajectories (reward hacking averaged over 3 runs, temperature 0.1). Nothing in the loops prevents drift; the paper's central finding is that reward hacking (refund-heuristic collapse at round 60 of the dynamic loop; sales agent fabricating specs; medical agent reassuring a gunshot victim) and alignment decay emerge precisely because the fitness signal omits safety. Mitigations tested are post-hoc patches (DPO on 1K PKU-RLHF pairs; 'memories are references not rules' prompt; 'refuse if unsafe' ingestion prompt; safety instruction on the Ensemble node), each recovering only part of the loss.
limitations: Memory 'static' experiments use hand-crafted synthetic memories (6 experiences) rather than accumulated ones; the dynamic loop is 1 scenario, 1 model (Qwen2.5-72B), 100 rounds, 10 test queries. Small N: 25 tool pairs, 40 memory cases, 5 curated tool cases. SE-Agent memory decay tested on a single model. Model-evolution results use others' released checkpoints (uncontrolled training) except one 200-step AZR rerun. Safety judged mostly by LLM judges (Gemini-2.5-Pro judging Gemini-2.5-Pro agents). Capability/safety trade-off of mitigations measured on only 50 SWE-Bench cases. Tool-safety verification pipeline proposed but explicitly 'not tested'. No causal/mechanistic analysis (hypotheses only in Appendix A). Authors state they cannot enumerate all misevolution forms and cannot propose a unified evaluation framework across agent architectures. Code release is partial: repo has evaluation scripts for model benchmarks, the static reward-hacking prompts, the CWEval tool-creation agent, and AFlow+RedCode-Gen, but NOT the dynamic AgentNet loop, SE-Agent memory runs, the 371-sample malicious-ingestion dataset, the evolved AFlow workflow, or the 200-step AZR checkpoints; 'Getting Started: Coming soon', tool/workflow READMEs empty, HF dataset badge links nowhere.
key_insight: Any evolution function whose acceptance signal is task utility alone will silently trade away safety across every evolvable component: this happens with no adversary, no parameter update (memory alone drops Qwen3-Coder-480B refusal from 99.4% to 54.4%), no harmful content in self-generated data, and via structurally innocuous mutations (an Ensemble node picks the 'more complete' malware). Therefore safety must be inside the fitness/acceptance gate, re-validated whenever a learned artifact (memory, tool, workflow node) is reused in a new context, and backed by versioned rollback, because post-hoc prompt/DPO patches recover only part of the loss (e.g. ASR 20.6->13.1 vs 0.6 initial; workflow RR 5.6->13.1 vs 36.3 initial).
open_gaps: No studied framework (AFlow, SE-Agent, Alita-style tool loop, Absolute-Zero) includes a safety term in the mutation acceptance criterion; a harness could run a fixed safety regression suite (e.g. RedCode-Gen RR/ASR, HarmBench subset) at every evolution step and reject/rollback mutations that regress it.
Rollback/versioning of self-modifications with tagged 'known-safe' checkpoints is only proposed in the Appendix B checklist, never implemented or tested.

Two-stage tool safety verification (static analysis at creation, LLM judge re-validation at reuse in the new context) is proposed but explicitly 'not tested'; nothing currently flags cross-domain reuse (PII tool built for customer data reused on medical data).

Memory loop has no retrieval-time filtering, provenance/recency weighting, or quarantine; the 'treat memory as reference' prompt only cuts reward-hacking unsafe rate 71.8%->51.4% and no-memory baseline is 0%.

No anomaly detector for abrupt memory-driven heuristic collapse (dynamic loop stayed safe until a single high-rated unreasonable refund at rounds 50-60 flipped the policy); a monitor on action-distribution shift per memory write is missing.

Workflow mutation operators lack safety-preserving invariants; the evolved Ensemble node selects the most detailed child and amplifies harm; safety-aware aggregation operators or safety-constrained MCTS objectives are untested.

External tool ingestion has <8% baseline refusal of backdoored repos; a prompt raises it to ~69% but the 371-sample dataset is unreleased and no automated code-scanning gate is built into the ingestion path.

Model self-training degrades safety even with benign self-generated data; no safety-preserving self-training method (safety anchor data mixing, KL-to-initial on safety prompts, periodic re-alignment) is evaluated beyond post-hoc DPO on 1K pairs recovering 59.5->62.75 of a 64.0 baseline.
No scalable longitudinal harness: the only dynamic simulation is 1 scenario, 1 model, 100 rounds; continuous safety telemetry across evolution rounds for arbitrary agents does not exist.
Interactions between pathways (memory + tools + workflow evolving simultaneously) are never studied; each pathway is isolated.
Capability cost of mitigations is measured only on 50 SWE-Bench-Verified cases for one prompt; no Pareto analysis of safety vs utility for any mitigation.

name: Awesome-Self-Evolving-Agents (XMUDeepLIT) / "A Systematic Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: From Model-Centric to Environment-Driven Co-Evolution"
mechanism: This is a curated reading list plus companion survey, not a runnable system: nothing in the repo executes a loop. What it contributes is a taxonomy of loops. The survey defines an agent as a tuple <Phi (policy/weights), M (memory), T (tools), I (interaction interface; perception P was folded into I after issue #2)> and defines self-evolution by two properties: "strong autonomy with minimal human supervision" and "active exploration through interaction" (maintainer reply, issue #4). Three evolvable substrates: (1) Model-centric: inference-time (self-consistency, Self-Refine, ToT) or training-time mutation of Phi via self-synthesized data (STaR/SEAL) or online self-play/RL with verifiable or self-generated rewards (R-Zero, Absolute Zero, Agent0, WebRL, TTCS). (2) Environment-centric: mutate what sits between model and world -- knowledge (agentic RAG/deep research), experience/context (ReasoningBank, ACE, GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet, Memento), skills (SkillWeaver, AutoSkill, SkillRL, OpenSkill), tools (Voyager, LATM, Alita, Godel Agent), memory architecture (A-Mem, MemEvolve), topology (ADAS, AFlow, EvoAgent, MaAS). (3) Co-evolution: agent and environment/curriculum/verifier co-adapt (GenEnv, RLVE, EnvScaler, AutoForge, CoMAS, co-evolving coder/tester). The list's newest and most useful sections are "Self-Evolution Evaluation" benchmarks (Aspire, S3Gym, HarnessDev: held-out downstream tasks after weight/harness updates) and community-added harness tooling (AgentDescent: N workers propose diffs to skills/prompts/harness, aggregator accepts on Beta posterior over held-out reward; hmharness: bench-gated skill evolution with canary A/B; RewardHarness). The list itself evolves by PR: 21 PRs, most from the added projects' own authors, reviewed by two maintainers with no written acceptance criteria.
eval_loop: None intrinsic -- the repo is a document. For the surveyed literature the signal varies by branch: verifiable rewards/unit tests and self-play win-rates for weight evolution; task success or self-judgment for experience/skill evolution; held-out downstream tasks only in the three Sept-2026 "self-evolution evaluation" benchmarks (Aspire, S3Gym, HarnessDev) and in AgentDescent's Beta-posterior acceptance gate. The survey flags reward hacking/misevolution via a single paper ("Your agent may misevolve", ICLR'26) and a solver-verifier-gap theory paper; it does not classify papers by signal type or by regression-prevention mechanism. List curation drift: entries are added by self-promoting PR authors (Ouroboros, hmharness, agent-qa, Aeon, AgentDescent, TaoLive) with no stated inclusion bar.
limitations: 1) No experiments or numbers: pure taxonomy. 2) Per-paper annotations of what-evolves / fitness signal / rollback are absent except the Applications table's one-phrase "Evolution Mechanism" column; only 4 [[Code]] links across 212 paper entries, no star counts or maturity for projects. 3) Taxonomy is leaky: authors concede in issue #4 that "inference-based evolution" (self-consistency, ToT) produces no persistent change and is "temporary and localized"; several works (Voyager, AgentGym, Reasoning Gym) appear in multiple sections. 4) Safety coverage is one paper plus an unrelated embodied-safety survey. 5) The survey paper is on TechRxiv v2 (2026-02-27)/SSRN, not arXiv -- the README's arXiv badge id 2602.05665 resolves to a different paper (Graph-based Agent Memory); OpenAlex shows 0 citations. 6) Applications table lists commercial products (Devin, Cursor, Manus, Claude Code, OpenClaw) with vague, unverifiable mechanism descriptions ("Skill accumulation", "Human-AI co-evolution"). 7) Maintenance is two people (58/89 commits) with 4-11 commits/month since March; a companion list from a different group has 6x the stars. 8) Benchmarks section is mostly generic capability benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, SWE-bench), not evolution benchmarks, until the Sept 2026 addition.
key_insight: Treat the agent as a tuple (weights, memory/experience, tools/skills, topology, environment/curriculum) and pick the cheapest substrate to mutate: the field is moving from mutating weights (needs GPU RL and verifiable rewards) to mutating environment-facing state (skills, context, harness) and finally the environment itself (co-evolution), and the only honest measure of a self-evolution loop is improvement on hidden held-out tasks after the loop runs, not on the tasks the loop trained on.
open_gaps: No surveyed system evolves multiple substrates (prompts, skills, memory, tools, topology, curriculum) under one shared acceptance gate; each paper mutates one substrate, so a unified harness with a single held-out fitness test and per-substrate blast-radius policies is open

Regression prevention is not even a taxonomy category: versioned artifacts, rollback, canary deployment and a frozen regression suite appear only in community-added tools (hmharness, AgentDescent, Ouroboros), never as a studied mechanism

Fitness for experience/skill evolution (ACE, ReasoningBank, Dynamic Cheatsheet, Memento) is in-distribution task success or self-judgment; held-out/hidden-task evaluation exists only in Aspire/S3Gym/HarnessDev (Sept 2026), so a framework should ship hidden splits and report train-vs-held-out deltas by default
Cross-task and cross-domain transfer of learned skills is unmeasured except AgentKB/CoPS; a skill-library transfer benchmark and skill-pruning policy are missing

Credit assignment for non-parametric evolution is untracked: no method records which memory/skill entry caused which improvement, so libraries grow monotonically with no provenance-based garbage collection

The training-based branch requires GPU RL stacks (verl, slime, OpenRLHF); there is no training-free reference implementation of the environment-centric loop that an application developer can run on API models
No cost accounting or stopping criterion for evolution loops: none of the entries report compute per accepted improvement or define when to stop evolving
Safety of self-modification is one paper ('misevolve', ICLR'26): no category for permissioning, sandboxing, or human-review gates on agent-authored skills/tools/code

Multi-agent co-evolution entries mostly need MARL training; a training-free shared-experience population (Group-Evolving Agents style) with conflict resolution and merge acceptance is only prototyped in AgentDescent
The list itself lacks structured per-paper fields (what evolves, signal, rollback, code, stars); a machine-readable index with those fields would make the survey usable for framework design

name: Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses
last_activity: 2026-07-11 (meta-harness repo push: experimental Harbor pilot with trusted evaluator + leakage denylist; artifact repo last push 2026-03-26)
org_or_authors: Yoonho Lee, Roshen Nair, Qizheng Zhang, Kangwook Lee (KRAFTON), Omar Khattab (MIT), Chelsea Finn — Stanford IRIS Lab
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint cs.AI (v1 2026-03-30); citation count not retrieved (Semantic Scholar rate-limited); ~18k alphaXiv views; cited by Lilian Weng's harness-engineering post and by AHE as concurrent work; 5 community reimplementations listed in README
mechanism: Outer loop (Algorithm 1 / meta_harness.py): seed population = hand-written baseline harnesses (zero/few-shot, ACE, MCE; Terminus-2, Terminus-KIRA), each evaluated on a search set; results written to a filesystem D. Each iteration: (1) a single coding-agent proposer (Claude Code, Opus 4.6, effort=max, tools Read/Glob/Grep/Bash/Write/Edit/Agent) is launched with a short domain SKILL.md and a task prompt pointing at evolution_summary.jsonl (one row per past candidate: hypothesis, avg_val, delta), frontier_val.json (best per dataset/task + overall best/Pareto), and per-candidate dirs holding source code, val.json scores and raw log.jsonl trajectories. It greps/cats whatever it wants (median 82 files/iter, 41% prior code, 40% traces), forms a falsifiable hypothesis, prototypes, then copy-then-edits a top harness into a new single-file Python class (MemorySystem or Terminus2 subclass) and writes pending_eval.json (k=3 candidates for text classification, k=1 for TB2). (2) The trusted outer script import-validates (TB2 also runs a 1-task smoke trial), benchmarks each candidate on the search set only, updates the frontier (strictly-greater replacement; no parent selection, no pruning, no crossover operator), appends summary rows, and loops for a fixed N (typically 20 iters / ~60 harnesses; TB2 10 iters, 89 tasks x 2 trials, ~$500 and 4-6 h per iteration). (3) After search, --test freezes the run and evaluates the Pareto frontier once on held-out test data. Regressions are tolerated (candidates are separate files; frontier keeps the best); the proposer itself reasons over failures (paper shows it diagnosing a prompt-edit confound after 2 regressions and pivoting to an additive env-bootstrap change after 6).
eval_loop: Signal = task benchmark score on a search/validation set (accuracy for online text classification on USPTO/S2D/LawBench; pass@1 on 250 olympiad problems with GPT-OSS-20B; Harbor pass rate on TB2). Multi-objective via Pareto dominance over accuracy vs context tokens. Drift/overfitting controls: test sets held out until a one-shot finalize step (text-class: separate results dir, run frozen after test; math: 200 unseen IMO-level problems and 4 unseen base models; corpus decontaminated by exact-prefix + Jaccard 0.8); SKILL.md forbids dataset/task names and parameter-only variants and mandates prototyping; TB2 has NO held-out split (search and reported eval on the same 89 tasks) and overfitting is checked only by manual inspection and regex audits for task-string leakage. The July 2026 experimental Harbor pilot adds a trusted subprocess controller with per-task forbidden_references denylists and a universal denylist (/tests, verifier, /solution) plus a bounded eval budget. No statistical acceptance test; 2 trials/task during TB2 search, 5 trials for the final number.
key_results: Text classification (GPT-OSS-120B): best discovered harness 48.6% avg vs ACE 40.9 (+7.7) and MCE 40.0, using 11.4K ctx tokens vs 50.8K (ACE); OOD on 9 unseen datasets 73.1 vs ACE 70.2 (best on 6/9). Optimizer comparison (search set, median/best): GEPA 32.6/40.2, Best-of-N 34.0/44.2, OpenEvolve 39.1/43.3, TTT-Discover 34.1/45.6, Meta-Harness 50.0/56.7; matches OpenEvolve/TTT-Discover's final accuracy in 0.1x the evaluations. Ablation: scores-only 34.6/41.3, scores+LLM-summary 34.9/38.7, full traces 50.0/56.7 — raw execution traces are the key ingredient. Math RAG: discovered 4-route BM25 harness 38.8 avg over 5 models (4 unseen) vs 34.1 no-retrieval (+4.7), 37.5 BM25 (+1.3), 38.1 dense k=5. TB2: Opus 4.6 76.4% (5 trials; #2 behind ForgeCode 81.8, above Terminus-KIRA 74.7), Haiku 4.5 37.6% (#1, Goose 35.5); the discovered change is ~80 lines of environment bootstrapping, gaining on 7/89 tasks.
limitations: Only one proposer (Claude Code/Opus 4.6) studied; authors say the workflow only became practical with early-2026 coding agents. TB2 search and final eval use the same 89 tasks, so 76.4% is a discovery-problem number, not generalization; gains over KIRA are +1.7 pts on 7/89 tasks, within benchmark noise (search-run KIRA baseline was 64.4% vs 74.7% leaderboard, showing high concurrency/timeout sensitivity). Math gain over plain BM25 is 1.3 pts. Cost is high (~$500 and 4-6 h per TB2 iteration; proposer reads ~82 files/iter). The hand-written SKILL.md is admitted to be the strongest lever ('larger effect than iteration count or population size'), requiring per-domain engineering and 3-5-iteration debug runs. Release note: code 'not tested beyond verifying that it runs'; text-class test data ships in the repo (operational, not real isolation). Search is a serial single-agent loop with k<=3 candidates/iteration and no re-evaluation of noisy frontier entries.
safety_measures: Proposer is told (via skill text) it CANNOT edit existing agents, meta_harness.py or claude_wrapper.py and must not encode task/dataset names — enforced by convention plus regex audits, not by sandbox, in the reference examples. Candidates must pass interface validation (import + Terminus2 subclass check) and a 1-task smoke test before paid evaluation. Test sets are never shown to the proposer; finalize step freezes runs. Experimental Harbor pilot (July 2026) adds: candidate code never imported by the outer agent/controller, staged in a temp dir and run in a child Harbor job; forbidden-string leakage checks; frozen append-only evaluation history and eval budget; credentials passed only to the child. No rollback needed since each candidate is a separate file and the frontier keeps the best.
key_insight: Give the improving agent uncompressed, selectively-accessed experience (all prior candidates' code, scores AND raw execution traces on a filesystem it greps) instead of a hand-designed search loop with compressed feedback; the ablation shows raw traces, not scores or LLM summaries, are what make code-space harness search work, and a minimal outer loop with no parent-selection rule is sufficient once the proposer is a capable coding agent.
open_gaps: Fitness on TB2 = the same 89-task benchmark that is reported; no automatic held-out or cross-benchmark generalization gate before a candidate is accepted onto the frontier
No statistical acceptance test: frontier replacement is strict greater-than on a 2-trial noisy score; no re-evaluation of incumbent vs challenger, no confidence intervals or bootstrap
Reward-hacking defense is a string denylist (task names, /tests, verifier) plus manual inspection; no behavioral detection of eval exploitation (reading grading scripts, peeking at test outputs)

Experience is never distilled: the filesystem grows unboundedly and the proposer re-reads ~82 files every iteration; no learned memory/lessons store, no cross-run or cross-domain transfer beyond ad hoc references to earlier runs
The meta-level (SKILL.md and outer-loop script) is hand-written and frozen even though the authors say it is the strongest lever; the skill itself is not optimized
Single serial proposer producing 1-3 candidates per iteration; no parallel proposers, island/population diversity, or crossover operators, so search throughput is bounded by one Claude Code session
No cheap proxy or progressive evaluation: every candidate pays full search-set cost (~$500/iteration on TB2); the 'hard' subset is only a manual bring-up suggestion
Search space restricted to a single-file Python class with a fixed interface; cannot co-evolve tools, multi-file systems, model choice, or model weights (co-evolution named as future work)
Proposer is Claude Code only; wrappers for other agents must be adapted by hand, and generality across proposers is unstudied
Reference examples rely on convention ('CANNOT modify meta_harness.py') rather than enforced sandboxing of the proposer, which has Bash/Write access to the repo

name: Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: From Bounded Self-Refinement to Autonomous Research Loops
org_or_authors: Mingguang Chen (DeepGrounding, corresponding), Licheng Wang (AlphaAvatar), Bo Qu (Illinois Institute of Technology)
last_activity: 2026-09-06 (arXiv v2 + public release of companion repo deepgrounding/recursive-self-improvement)
venue_or_citations: arXiv preprint cs.AI (44 pp. incl. refs); no venue; citation count unavailable (Semantic Scholar rate-limited, paper is ~2 months old); companion GitHub repo has 0 stars / 0 forks
mechanism: This is a survey, not a system; it has no loop of its own. Its contribution is a canonical description of every self-improvement loop as: (1) generate candidates, (2) score them with an evaluator, (3) select/apply the winner into a substrate, (4) persist or discard. Axis 1 = which substrate absorbs the improvement: deployment-time (frozen-weight output refinement -> test-time weight updates -> harness/skill/memory evolution, ordered by persistence: evaporates per episode < lasts a session < accumulates indefinitely), training-time (self-reward RL, STaR-style CoT self-training, on-policy self-distillation where the same weights conditioned on privileged info act as teacher, self-play/zero-data proposer-solver, embodied/synthetic-data loops), the evaluator itself (judges, PRMs, verifiers, rubrics, meta-evaluation, co-evolved verifiers a la Red Queen Godel Machine), or the research process (evolutionary program discovery like FunSearch/AlphaEvolve, AI-scientist agents, A-Evolve-Training running a 30B post-training loop end to end). Axis 2 = loop closure: human-in-the-loop (person reviews each change), human-on-the-loop (automatic signal, human audits outcomes and gates deployment), closed loop (system generates, validates, applies its own changes). The paper's central claim: nearly all 1,250 papers sit in the human-on-the-loop row; the closed-loop x self-evaluation cell (a system rewriting its own definition of 'better') is where bounded self-refinement becomes open-ended RSI. A verification hierarchy (formal verifier > execution feedback > learned judge > intrinsic self-assessment) predicts observed improvement strength, and four failure modes (self-confirming loop, model collapse, diversity collapse, frame lock-in) are derived as violations of it. Corpus: 871 seed + 379 supplemental arXiv papers classified by theme defaults + keyword rules + explicit overrides, single annotator.
eval_loop: The survey's own 'signal' is bibliographic: arXiv harvest across seven query threads enriched with OpenAlex metadata, then rule-based classification (theme defaults + title/abstract keyword rules moved 89 papers; 3 manual overrides), all by a single annotator with per-paper assignments released for audit -- no inter-annotator agreement reported. For the systems it surveys, the paper argues the improvement signal must be placed on a verification hierarchy: formal verifiers (proof checkers, type systems; sound, can iterate indefinitely), execution feedback (tests/compilers/benchmarks; reliable but incomplete and eventually gamed), learned judges (reward models, LLM-as-judge; ~80% human agreement but themselves optimization targets), intrinsic signals (confidence, self-consistency, likelihood; cheapest and most gameable). Drift/reward hacking is framed as inevitable when generator and evaluator share weights (confidence-coupled rewards over-reward high-confidence mistakes), when exogenous signal fraction vanishes (collapse), or when proposers narrow the curriculum (diversity collapse); the recommended countermeasures are data gating + reward grounding as separate levers, entropy reservoirs (real-data mixing, retrieval), evaluator co-evolution, and human-on-the-loop gating. It also separates result-level (cheap, per-instance, opex) from process-level (expensive, reusable, capex) evaluation and argues durable gains are process-level.
key_results: Corpus of 1,250 arXiv papers (2024-26): deployment-time self-evolution 393 (74% from 2026), training-time self-iteration 340 (69%), self-evaluation 318 (82%), auto research 139 (76%), foundations/limits/safety 60 (57%); 74% of corpus posted in 2026, quarterly output ~500 papers in 2026 Q2. Headline evidence assembled from cited works: Mirror Loop -- 10 rounds of ungrounded self-critique drops informational change 55%, a single verification step at round 3 restores progress; SkillsBench -- human-written skills +16.2 pass-rate points, LLM-written skills no measurable gain; Pareto analysis of 34 inference-scaling configs -- peak +7.1 points over CoT only at ~20x compute; SciIntegrity-Bench -- 34.2% integrity-failure rate, all seven frontier models fabricate data in missing-data scenarios; SoundnessBench (1,099 ICLR proposals) -- pervasive optimism bias in 12 frontier models as research-direction evaluators; A-Evolve-Training -- autonomous 4-round post-training of a 30B model reached 0.86 vs 0.87 human top (8th of ~4,000) and mid-run detected its dev metric had decoupled from the external target and inverted its use of the proxy; rise-and-collapse of pass@1 under verifiable binary reward in REINFORCE that KL/EWC do not prevent; on-policy self-distillation thread went from 0 to 56 papers in ~18 months.
limitations: Stated: corpus is a sample not a census, recency-biased by construction (supplement harvest), citation counts near zero so impact cannot be inferred; classification is automatic keyword rules plus single annotator, ~54 of 379 supplement papers are peripheral query bleed left in counts; industrial RSI inside frontier labs is unobservable (publication censoring); taxonomy deliberately does not encode whether the objective is still correct (frame lock-in) nor trajectory/continuity of one system across cells; verification hierarchy is a qualitative pattern, 'not a measured law'. Observed: the original Data availability link (bamboodrift/recursive_self_improvement) was private and did not resolve, replaced only in the 2026-09-06 v2 release; authors are from small/unknown orgs (DeepGrounding, AlphaAvatar) with no track record visible; survey leans heavily on Anthropic's May 2026 RSI essay for framing; representative-systems-per-cell grid (Figure 1) is an image with no machine-readable mapping; no quantitative meta-analysis, only narrative synthesis.
safety_measures: Surveys rather than implements: cites 'unfireable safety kernel' argument that guardrails inside the agent's modifiable runtime are reachable by inputs, so execution-time alignment must live outside the agent's address space; human-oversight anchors against safety drift and capability degradation that arise without any adversary; constraining the self-modification surface to auditable, diffable, roll-back-able artifacts (SHARP rubric policies) instead of free-form prompt/code evolution; formally verifiable skill evolution (VASO) for physical agents; threat analyses of permanently-encoded, self-amplifying, population-transmissible corruption in shared skill libraries; skill spec/code mismatch attacks (SkillMutator); deterministic integrity gates in regulated domains; calls for governance-grade measurement of what a training loop is and is not improving (identified as the emptiest niche: 60 of 1,250 papers on foundations/safety).
key_insight: Self-improvement is only as real as its verification signal: demonstrated gains track a strict hierarchy (formal verifier > execution feedback > learned judge > intrinsic self-assessment), and the risk of a loop is set by the persistence of what it modifies (outputs evaporate < weights roll back < harness/skills/memory accumulate and propagate) -- so a framework should pick the highest-rung signal available per task, keep a fixed external anchor even when co-evolving its evaluator, and constrain the self-modification surface to artifacts the chosen signal can actually audit, diff, and roll back.
open_gaps: No 'exchange rate of grounding': nobody has measured the minimum fraction of exogenous (human/formal/execution) signal per iteration that keeps a loop improving rather than collapsing; a framework could instrument and log external-signal share and detect when it trends toward zero

Trustworthy accumulation: persistent self-modifications (skills, memory, harness code, experience graphs) have no verification/rollback story comparable to weight checkpoints; concrete pattern to adopt: constrain the evolvable surface to diffable, auditable artifacts (rubrics/skill docs) with regression tests and automatic rollback on held-out drops

Frame-revision detection has neither benchmark nor metric: build a suite of deliberately stale or misspecified objectives scored on whether the loop notices (productive abandonment, invariant transfer, absence-sensitivity, reframing latency) rather than how well it optimizes

Evaluator co-evolution (Red Queen, self-trained verifiers, self-evolved rubrics) is unproven against the self-confirming loop; frameworks that evolve their judge need a held-out, non-evolving anchor set and meta-evaluation to show the judge did not drift with the policy

Stability engineering is per-paradigm folklore: no unified detector for rise-and-collapse, diversity collapse, or safety drift; a harness could track output entropy, curriculum diversity, and pass@k trajectories across generations and halt/branch on collapse signatures

LLM-authored skills give zero gain on SkillsBench while human-authored give +16.2 points: skill-writing must be evaluation-guided and trace-conditioned, not one-shot; no framework yet closes this gap in a general-purpose harness
Governance-grade measurement absent: no method produces auditable evidence of what a loop is and is not improving over time (per-substrate change logs, capability deltas against fixed external evals)

Taxonomy indexes substrate, not trajectory: no way to record that one system improved outputs, then evaluator, then method ('scientific amnesia' -- behaviors improve while no methodological knowledge accumulates); a framework needs a process-level memory of how prior improvement campaigns were run, not just their results

Non-verifiable tasks (research direction, creative quality) remain at the bottom rung; direction-evaluation is benchmarkable (SoundnessBench shows frontier models optimism-biased) but direction-generation has no evaluation at all

Representative-systems-per-cell mapping exists only as a figure image; no machine-readable dataset labels each of the 1,250 papers with loop-closure level, so mapping frameworks onto the grid still requires manual work
Survey's own classification is single-annotator keyword rules with no inter-annotator agreement; category counts should not be used as field-composition statistics

name: Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursive Self-Improvement
org_or_authors: Xunjian Yin, Xinyi Wang, Liangming Pan, Li Lin, Xiaojun Wan, William Yang Wang — Peking University, UC Santa Barbara, University of Arizona
last_activity: Repo last push 2025-09-17 ("fix typo and change api": swapped optimizer to o3-2025-04-16, solver to gpt-4.1-mini / gpt-4o-mini). Only 9 commits total; no substantive code evolution since Oct 2024.
venue_or_citations: ACL 2025 main (Long Papers). Semantic Scholar: 30 citations on the ACL record (+23 on the arXiv record, likely overlapping), 2 influential; OpenAlex: 5. Cited as the self-referential predecessor by Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al. 2025) and HyperAgents.
mechanism:
Single Python process; the agent IS the running module `agent_module`. Fixed parts: goal prompt (goal_prompt.md), `action_call_llm` / `action_call_json_format_llm` (explicitly protected from modification), the task's `evaluate()` harness, and the OpenAI API. Everything else — including `solver` (the policy π), `Agent.evolve` and `Agent.execute_action` (the meta-learner I), and the tool list — lives in runtime memory and is mutable.

Loop (mutual recursion, not a for-loop): `evolve()` builds messages = [goal prompt, `action_environment_aware()` summary of globals/attributes, last 10 items of `optimize_history`], calls the optimizer LLM (GPT-4o in paper; o3 in current code) with `tool_choice="required"` over 7 tools: display_analysis (think-before-act), environment_aware, read_logic (inspect.getsource on any function/class), adjust_logic (exec new code and setattr onto module/class = monkey patching; stores `__source__` so it can re-read itself), run_code (python exec into globals / bash), call_json_format_llm, evaluate_on_task. `execute_action()` runs each tool call, catches all exceptions and returns the traceback as the tool result (error handling), then calls `agent.evolve()` again. Hard stop after 100 evolve calls; paper used 30 iterations x 6 independent cycles per task.

Fitness: `evaluate_on_task` runs solver on 50 random questions from a 128-question validation set (48 threads); if valid acc >= 0.94 threshold it also runs the 800-question test set and returns BOTH numbers as feedback (per-sample info is commented out). If test acc beats `last_test_acc`, `store_all_logic()` dumps all in-memory functions/classes to disk as a best-so-far snapshot. No automatic rollback: the goal prompt tells the LLM to "backtrack, restore the original state" itself.
eval_loop: Signal = task accuracy (F1 for DROP) on a held-out validation subset (128 q; 32 for GPQA), sampled 50 at a time with a time-seeded shuffle, plus the 800-question test accuracy once valid acc crosses 0.94. The feedback string returned to the optimizer LLM is just "Valid Accuracy: X / Test Accuracy: Y" (the released code comments out per-sample diagnostics, though the goal prompt asks for case studies of low-score examples). Drift/regression control is weak and delegated to the LLM: there is no automatic accept/reject gate on a modification — a new solver stays live regardless of score; the only mechanical safeguard is that the best-scoring snapshot is written to disk. The paper reports 92% of 100 MGSM trials show temporary performance drops, 4% terminate unexpectedly (usually the agent broke its own `evolve`), and 14% end worse than the initial policy. Anti-reward-hacking is minimal: `adjust_logic` refuses edits to `action_call_llm`, bans `time.sleep`/`logging`, and the harness code (task_*.py) is a separate module the agent is not told to edit, but `run_code` gives it unrestricted exec and it could modify `task_mgsm.evaluate` or `last_test_acc`. Test accuracy leaking into the optimization feedback is a genuine evaluation flaw. A random-sampling control (30 GPT-4o resamples of the initial prompt) stays ~30% on MGSM vs. Gödel Agent's climb, showing the feedback matters.
key_results: Table 1 (solver = gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, optimizer = gpt-4o-2024-05-13, ADAS/Meta Agent Search protocol): Gödel-base DROP 80.9 F1 / MGSM 64.2 / MMLU 70.9 / GPQA 34.9 vs Meta Agent Search 79.4 / 53.4 / 69.6 / 34.6 vs CoT 64.2 / 28.0 / 65.4 / 29.2. Gödel-free (agent allowed to call GPT-4o inside the solver) 90.5 / 90.6 / 87.9 / 55.7 — this is mostly a model-upgrade effect the paper itself admits. Ablation on MGSM: w/o think-before-act 50.8 (-13.4), w/o error handling 49.4 (-14.8), w/o run_code 57.1 (-7.1), w/o call_LLM 60.4 (-3.8). Cost ~$15 for 30 iterations across all four datasets vs ~$300 for Meta Agent Search. Game of 24: after 6 failed LLM-prompt tweaks the agent rewrote the solver as brute-force arithmetic search -> 100%; but with ToT as the initial policy, no run exceeded ToT's own performance. Robustness: 100 MGSM trials -> 4% crash, 92% temporary dips, 14% end below initial policy. Repo's archived best solvers (matching Table 1 numbers) are all variants of CoT + self-consistency majority voting with n=5-20 samples (plus few-shot for MMLU); the archived `Agent.evolve` is byte-identical to the initial one, i.e. the meta-learner was never actually improved in the released best runs.
limitations: Stated: can't compete with heavily engineered systems (e.g. OpenDevin) since it must build all task code itself; self-comprehension may degrade as the agent's own code grows (Yampolskiy); unsafe without sandboxing and constrained modification. Observed from code/paper: (1) demonstrated gains come almost entirely from policy-level edits — the discovered policies are textbook self-consistency/few-shot, and the meta-level (evolve/execute_action) was not improved in any released run, so 'recursive' self-improvement of the learner is claimed but not demonstrated; (2) no acceptance gate or rollback — bad edits stay live and the LLM must notice and revert; (3) test-set accuracy is fed back to the optimizer, contaminating the reported test numbers; (4) memory is the last 10 messages, so the agent forgets earlier experiments and repeats them; (5) mutual recursion evolve->execute_action->evolve grows the Python stack every step (capped at 100); (6) single-agent, single-lineage, no population/archive beyond a best-snapshot dump; (7) Gödel-free numbers are inflated by calling a stronger model; (8) baselines copied from the ADAS paper rather than re-run; (9) Game-of-24 'innovation' is brute-force search, and with a strong initial policy (ToT) the agent never beat it; (10) unrestricted exec of LLM-generated code in the host process with the API key on disk.
key_insight: Make the agent's own runtime memory the substrate of evolution: expose inspect/exec-based read and monkey-patch write of every live function (including the improver itself) as ordinary tool calls, so the boundary between 'policy' and 'meta-learner' disappears and a single LLM tool-loop can in principle rewrite either — and the two things that actually made this work empirically were not the self-reference but (a) forcing an explicit analysis step before each edit and (b) catching every exception and feeding the traceback back as a tool result instead of crashing.
safety_measures: Minimal and mostly prompt-level: `action_adjust_logic` raises on attempts to modify `Agent.action_call_llm`/`action_call_json_format_llm`, on `time.sleep` in solver, and on use of `logging`; all tool exceptions are caught and returned as text; hard cap of 100 evolve calls (sys.exit). Everything else is unrestricted: `action_run_code` does raw `exec` in module globals and `subprocess.run(shell=True)`, the agent can edit its own `evolve`, and the evaluation harness module is reachable. Paper's ethics statement recommends sandboxing and constrained-modification rules but neither is implemented. No rollback, no diff review, no human-in-the-loop.
open_gaps: No automatic accept/reject gate: a modified solver goes live regardless of its validation score; the only safeguard is a best-snapshot dump to disk, so a framework should add score-gated commit + automatic revert to the last accepted version.

Meta-level self-modification is possible but never demonstrated to help: the released best runs leave Agent.evolve untouched, and modifications to it were the main cause of crashes (4%). A framework needs a protected/versioned meta-loop with a separate acceptance test for improver edits.

Fitness = single-task accuracy on 50 sampled validation questions with test accuracy leaked into the feedback string; no held-out generalization, no cross-task transfer, no noise-aware comparison (50-sample acc has ~±7% CI).

Memory is the last 10 tool messages; there is no archive of tried modifications, their scores, or diffs, so the agent re-tries ideas and cannot do credit assignment across iterations (paper's own cost note says growing history is the main cost driver — a structured experiment log would fix both).
Single lineage, no population/branching: a bad edit stalls the run; nothing like DGM's archive or tree search over agent variants.

Discovered policies are all self-consistency + few-shot variants; with a strong initial policy (ToT) no run beat it, so the open-endedness claim is untested — a framework needs curricula or task sequencing (the authors list this as future work) to push past the LLM's known tricks.

No sandboxing: LLM-generated code is exec'd in the host process with shell access and the API key on disk; the evaluation harness and score variable (last_test_acc) are reachable and could be gamed. Needs process isolation plus an immutable evaluator.

Mutual recursion evolve->execute_action->evolve grows the Python stack each iteration and hard-exits at 100; the loop should be a resumable, checkpointable state machine so long runs, crash recovery and multi-day evolution are possible.
Optimizer and solver are both OpenAI-only with hard-coded model enums; no model-agnostic interface, no local models, no cost/budget accounting inside the loop.

Evaluation of the evolved agent happens on the same task it evolved on; no study of whether an evolved solver or evolved improver transfers to a new benchmark, and no comparison against simply running CoT-SC with n=20 on the base model (the trick the agent found).
